#6239. Hyatt Dining & Spa Awards: Are They Worth Redeeming Points For?

While the most popular way to redeem World of Hyatt points is for free night award redemptions, there are some lesser known ways to redeem Hyatt points. One of those is the ability to use points for Dining & Spa awards, which can be a surprisingly good deal.

This doesn’t get a lot of attention, and it’s particularly useful if you want to minimize your out-of-pocket when staying at a Hyatt property, while still indulging in on-property experiences.

Most people don’t realize that you can redeem World of Hyatt points toward the cost of on-property dining and spa experiences, and the value proposition can be surprisingly good. Specifically, you can redeem a certain number of points for a certain amount of credit to use toward on-property spending, even if you’re not staying at a Hyatt property. Let’s take a closer look at how this works.

Below is a chart showing the various redemption opportunities available with Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards, along with how much value you can potentially get per point:

As you can see, you can redeem anywhere from 1,000 points for a $10 credit, to 65,000 points for a $1,000 credit. The value per point ranges anywhere from 1.0 cents per point, to 1.54 cents per point.

1.54 cents per World of Hyatt point sounds like a solid deal. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, World of Hyatt points are worth 1.4 cents each, so this actually offers solid value, at least on the surface. Is there a catch, though?

The exact redemptions that are allowed vary by hotel, but generally you can expect that these awards can be used for food and beverage purchases, spa and salon services, and spa and salon retail items.

On top of that, when charged to a member’s guest room, the following charges may be eligible:

laundry, dry cleaning, telephone charges, pay-per-view movies, parking, gift/retail shop, service charges, taxes (not including room taxes) and gratuities

Meanwhile the following charges are expressly prohibited from being eligible:

room rates, room taxes, alcoholic beverages (in certain jurisdictions), catering or banquet charges, and casino charges

If you’re staying at a Hyatt then you should be able to redeem these awards for cumulative charges over the course of your stay. However, I’d recommend confirming this with the front desk at check-in, including which outlets would be eligible for these redemptions, since individual hotels could have different policies.

Not all Hyatt hotels participate in this program. Miraval, Unscripted by Hyatt, Hyatt Select, Destination by Hyatt, Hyatt Vacation Club properties, Hyatt Vivid, Bahia Principe, Impression by Secrets, Secrets, Dreams, Breathless, Zoëtry, Alua, Sunscape, and other Legacy AMR Collection resorts, as well as some Dream properties, do not participate. Furthermore, redemption of these certificates is limited to registered guests at Hyatt Zilara, Hyatt Ziva, and Hyatt Studios properties.

To be positive, you can search participating properties at this page.

You don’t need to redeem for these certificates in advance, but rather the World of Hyatt member should just inform the Hyatt employee at the eligible outlet that they’d like to redeem points toward their purchase at the outset. You’ll need to have your membership information, and should then be asked how many points you want to redeem.

If you’re a registered guest at a hotel then you can apply one of these at check-out toward multiple purchases over the course of a stay. If you’re not a registered guest then you’ll have to settle your folio at the particular outlet you’re at.

There are a few other things to potentially be aware of:

On the surface, being able to redeem World of Hyatt points for up to ~1.54 cents toward the cost of a purchase is a solid deal. Is it exceptional? No. But as a way of essentially “cashing out” your points to offset cash costs I think it’s very good.

I do think it’s important to create a more realistic valuation of these redemptions, though. When you redeem these awards you’re forgoing the opportunity to earn points on these purchases:

As a Globalist member I earn 10.5x points per dollar spent, which I value at a return of ~15% (1.4 cents per point). That’s an opportunity cost that’s worth factoring in, so in reality, I’d adjust the maximum value from 1.54 cents to ~1.3 cents.

Personally, this isn’t how I’d redeem my World of Hyatt points, though I do think many people could find this to be worthwhile for a splurge:

World of Hyatt offers Dining & Spa awards, allowing members to redeem points for dining and spa experiences at most Hyatt properties. This has the potential to be a solid deal, as getting 1.54 cents per Hyatt point toward the cost of a purchase is a good redemption. However, do factor in the points you’re forgoing, which brings down the redemption value a bit.

While I wouldn’t say this is the best way to redeem Hyatt points, this could be worth it to lower how much cash you’ll pay for a Hyatt stay, especially at a secluded resort where you’re likely to spend most time on-property.

What do you make of Hyatt’s Dining & Spa awards? Could you see yourself redeeming points for them?

#6238. Marriott Earnings Call: New Upgrade List Encourages Elites To Pay For Better Rooms—But Puts Its Credit Card Cash Cow At Risk

Marriott earned $794 million in the third quarter, up from $728 million a year ago. They’re doing well. At the same time, I’ve been covering reports of layoffs in the customer service teams guests turn to when hotels won’t honor benefits. And on their earnings call, Marriott explained that its new elite upgrade list is being designed to preserve owners’ ability to sell upgrades. The company is getting better at monetizing Bonvoy. More than half its fee growth came from credit cards. But they’re spending down the trust that makes the program worth something in the first place. The hotel business has been good, outside of pockets like the Mideast. Marriott’s revenue per available room rose 6.5%. Adjusted earnings per share rose from $2.47 to $3.02, beating the $2.84 analysts expected. Marriott’s quarterly filing identifies $68 million in additional credit card fees compared with the same quarter last year. More than half of the increase in franchise fees comes from cards. Third Quarter Fee Growth   Increase   Share From Higher Card Fees Franchise fees   $131 million   52% Total gross fees   $184 million   37% I’ve covered owners’ unhappiness with these economics. Fifty-one owners representing about 1,000 hotels demanded better compensation for award stays. They’re supplying the rooms, Marriott sells them at a discount to Chase and American Express customers. The basic hotel loyalty bargain is a loop. Hotels pay into a program that rewards guests for stays. Those guests redeem points for more stays. Owners supply discounted award nights in exchange for a program that encourages customers to choose their hotels. A vacant room is cheap to give away. When an award guest doesn’t displace a paying customer, the hotel’s cost is mostly cleaning, utilities and whatever benefits it provides. Deep discounts make sense. But Marriott selling the points through Chase and American Express, using access to those discounted nights to monetize the owners’ inventory, infuriates some of them. As I’ve explained about bank payments for rewards, Marriott’s reported card fees aren’t everything the banks pay. Some money funds points and benefits. Some pays Marriott for licensing its brand and customer access. On the earnings call, Marriott pointed to the ways they’re appeasing owners: lower fees for Bonvoy higher reimbursement on high-demand award nights more flexible renovation requirements (letting owners allow the product to slip) a guest recommendation incentive. Marriott discussed its new upgrade lists. I covered the beta last month. Members can see their place in line and an estimate of upgrades matching their reservation. CEO Anthony Capuano told investors the feature would provide that visibility “while still preserving premium room upsell opportunities for our owners.” Showing you a position on a list doesn’t commit a room to you. A hotel can keep selling premium rooms while guests wait for complimentary upgrades. The later it commits the room, the longer it has to find someone willing to pay. Marriott hasn’t explained the beta’s inventory or clearance rules. They’re promising more visibility, but they aren’t saying hotels will release more rooms or confirm upgrades earlier. People who are lower on the list – and therefore less likely to get a free upgrade – become motivated to buy the upsell. Which, in turn, means fewer upgrade rooms available even at the top of the list. I’ve already described where Marriott’s technology investment is headed: selling room attributes and extras that guests used to receive as part of their stay or status. Better views, room locations and upgrades are going to become new opportunities for revenue generation. Selling a premium room is perfectly reasonable. But Bonvoy also encourages guests to concentrate their stays and spending to earn upgrades. And they’ll sell those same upgrades back to lower-tier elites for tens of dollars – prioritizing minor ducats over long-term value. Meanwhile, Capuano trumpeted 309 million Bonvoy members. I’m amazed anyone keeps repeating these enrollment numbers seriously. It means a guest signed up to get a lower (member) room rate. That tells us they wanted to pay less for the reservation they were already making. It says nothing about interest in Bonvoy or continued engagement. And the numbers are large because Marriott has a lot of hotels and rooms. I’ve reported on employees signing guests up who don’t even know about it, alongside hotel incentives worth as much as $10,000 a month for enrollment performance. Marriott intentionally does not share active members When I wrote about Chris Buckner taking over Bonvoy, I argued that his biggest opportunity was getting hotels to deliver the benefits members had already earned. Marriott’s business depends on guests starting their hotel search with Marriott. The brand is supposed to stand for a consistent product, and Bonvoy is supposed to make the brand sticky. That’s what lets Marriott deliver customers to owners as “leads” and charge for access to them. The reservation system doesn’t have value to sell to owners if guests stop trusting the hotels it displays. An individual owner can save money by denying breakfast or an upgrade. The damage gets spread across the whole portfolio. That hotel benefits from shirking on the program, while the program loses value. That’s why Marriott is supposed to enforce its promises. Yet they rarely seem to! I covered a breakfast dispute where the hotel closed the guest’s case seven times before finally paying the $100 benefit guarantee the guest was clearly due. In Marriott’s system, the hotel becomes the judge of complaints against it. . So, they learned from Delta’s earnings calls to not literally say the quiet part out loud and be explicitly evil. (“We’re gonna price-gouge the sh*t outta our customers!”) Huh. Wild.

At many properties, you need to have a Bonvoy number to get complimentary internet. There would be less Bonvoy members if they didn’t do this.

Also, always use a VPN, so that Bonvoy isn’t building a profile on your internet history.

I may be one of the most infrequent travelers, but I still remember the moments I signed on encouraged by desk staff to SPG when staying at the Sheraton Boston. I was immediately upgraded to a mini suite and got take out from the Kon TIki off the lobby and enjoyed every minute of my stay. What I lack in travel (due to work, caregiving, and health issues of my own) I make up for in loyalty and I never voted as the Shareholder I became based on my visits since a teen to the new (then) Sheraton Toronto. I am devastated by the ignorance of one of the most valued aspects imo of Marriott buying out Starwood, which I, as a tiny shareholder did not endorse. Heartbreaking that they have managed to destroy what was such a wonderful program. THe stupidity was obvious when they trashed all of our SPG numbers and did not provide new membership cards, not to mention how imo the related AMEX card art was well, I was going to say ugly, but I will say it is unappealing.

Unfortunately that is the norm in the US! Screw the customer! Let the hotel deny anything they want. I don’t expect any upgrade as a Platinum in the US. My number one complaint is breakfast in a High-end Marriott ! When you pay 800-1K or more? You don’t want continental breakfast! You don’t want them to act like they are doing you a favor giving you a donut! Most of all after you have spent all that money becoming so called the customer they want……then Marriot do as little as they can for that loyalty

I used to play a game called Roller Coaster Tycoon. One time I built an amusement park, where nobody could leave. At first it worked great. Then the customers became more and more unhappy, and no new people came to my amusement park.

More seriously, goodwill is an asset. Over the short run, you can increase profits by monetizing assets. However, over the long run, that will cause the goodwill to depreciate significantly. Famous brands that have no value any more are everywhere.

I am lifetime Platinum (Titanium currently). However, Marriott’s tricky app (in terms of pricing and cancellation date) (as I commented previously), removal of the ability to add guests, and other unfriendly acts are causing me to book elsewhere often.

For example, I am planning to meet my girlfriend near LAX. The LAX Marriott would normally be a good choice. However, we are flying in on different itineraries. If my plane is delayed, she won’t be able to check in. Going to book elsewhere.

As a Starwood transfer and current Marriott Lifetime Titanium (1700+ nights) I’m very disappointed with Marriott/Bonvoy. One problem might be that Marriott gives away upper tier status just by holding credit cards. When you can reach upper tier status basically just by holding credit cards, of course that status is going to be worthless.

I actually just reread Gary’s “Marriott Names A New Bonvoy Boss From JetBlue And The Points Guy—Will He Make Hotels Honor Your Benefits?” that he linked to above. It was a pretty good read. I am at the point where I do not expect any of the benefits to be honored. Enough said.

The whole craziness with Marriott and its ongoing process of nickel and diming its customers who buy into its “loyalty” program (Bonvoy) reminds me quite a bit of the “Master of the House” scene in the musical “Les Miserables” in which the innkeeper continually gouges and shortchanges his guests (with unexpected extra charges for everything) … and publicly brags about it. What Marriott does (and increasingly other so-called hospitality companies do) is at best shameful. Marriott and the others are selling you are for the most part illusions and wishful thinking for your blind “loyalty.”

The visible list mostly tells lower tier elites their odds. That’s exactly the moment the upsell starts to look tempting. Paying makes sense when the trip really needs the bigger room, a family stay or an anniversary, or when the paid upgrade is a small add on to the standard rate. If it’s just nice to have, Platinum and above can still sit on the list and see what clears.

The hotel’s own site or Google Hotels will show what that suite category costs booked outright for the same dates. FWIW that same Marriott can also price diff depending on which country you search from, since inventory and rates vary by market. Free tools like Arbitrica check it from around 195 countries and find kind of the lowest price in the world, which tells you fast whether the upsell is a deal. Then decide whether to pay now or gamble on the list

Marriott now views engaged loyalty members as suckers and adversaries. I’m lifetime platinum but generally tend to avoid their hotels.

@Christian — Yeah, maybe, just maybe… corporations should stop mistreating consumers…

The practical move now is to price the better room upfront. At a lot of Marriotts a Junior Suite is only $40 to $80 more a night on the booking engine, which beats waiting on a list that’s built to sell you the upgrade at check-in. FWIW a free tracker like HotelPriceTracker can watch that higher room category and email you when it drops, so you can rebook a refundable rate into the suite. If the gap stays big, take the standard room and keep the points for a stay where they’re worth more

#6237. Trump-backed ex-NFL reporter loses Senate race to progressive who vowed to 'rip ICE apart'

Republican Senate candidate Michele Tafoya spoke briefly, offering an uplifting message, after conceding to Democrat Peggy Flanagan.

Progressives scored a major victory in Minnesota, a state heavily targeted by the Trump administration in its immigration and anti-fraud crackdowns.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee, toppled former NFL sideline reporter and Republican nominee Michele Tafoya, stifling the GOP’s hopes of flipping the Land of 10,000 Lakes.

While her win over Tafoya, who was backed by President Donald Trump, is a positive for Democrats in their pursuit of power in the upper chamber, it's not necessarily a negative for Republicans, given that the seat was already blue.

PEGGY FLANAGAN VOWS TO 'RIP ICE APART' AFTER TOPPLING MODERATE DEM IN KEY SENATE BATTLE

Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, speaks during a primary election night party at First Avenue on Aug. 11, 2026, in Minneapolis. (Stephen Maturen/Getty Images)

Flanagan’s victory comes after the state of Minnesota and her former running mate, Gov. Tim Walz, were directly in the Trump administration’s crosshairs because of the sprawling, multibillion-dollar daycare fraud scandal that erupted earlier this year.

Given that several Somali immigrants were linked to the scandal, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) descended upon the state to enact Operation Metro Surge. That resulted in the deaths of two Minnesota residents, Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti, at the hands of federal immigration agents.

ICE’s actions in the state led to yet another government shutdown in Washington, D.C., and became a pointed rallying cry for her campaign and ammunition she used on the trail.

MN SENATE CANDIDATE RIPPED FOR BLAMING WALZ FOR FRAUD DESPITE BEING HIS #2: 'KNOWS SHE'S COOKED'

"We need to rip ICE apart and stop them from terrorizing our communities," Flanagan said shortly after winning her primary earlier this year. "And I know this. I know that we can fix our broken immigration system, secure the border, and create a real pathway to citizenship that aligns with our values."

Much of Tafoya’s campaign hinged on what role Flanagan played in the Minnesota fraud scheme and just how much she knew as a top official in the state.

"My opponent has been second in command in this state for eight years, drawing a taxpayer-funded paycheck," Tafoya said at a debate last month. "And what do we have to show for that? We have massive fraud, historic fraud. We have test scores down. We have crime spiking. We have a massive surplus turned into a deficit."

SLEEPER GOP CANDIDATE PUTS BLUE-LEANING STATE IN PLAY AS FRAUD SCANDAL SHADOWS DEMS

#6236. 59-Room Andaz Turks & Caicos At Grace Bay Opening April 2027, Now Bookable

The much delayed Andaz Turks & Caicos is getting closer to opening. The hotel has now moved forward the date as of which it’s accepting reservations, and we’ve also learned more details about the on-property amenities. Let’s cover all the details, as we’re potentially under five months from the opening…

The Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. This will mark Hyatt’s first hotel in Turks & Caicos, and the first Andaz property in the Caribbean. For that matter, it’s one of the only Andaz properties that’s currently in the pipeline outside of Asia, as the brand has really lost steam.

The 5.5-acre resort will offer four restaurants and bars, three outdoor pools, a spa, a kids club, a fitness center, tennis and pickleball courts, and more. The Andaz will be comprised of 59 rooms and 73 branded residences, so at least the hotel portion of the property will be boutique. It’ll be located directly on Grace Bay, known for offering one of the most beautiful stretches of beach in the Caribbean.

As far as the culinary concepts go, the Andaz Turks & Caicos will feature the following:

Runa Spa & Wellness, the spa at the Andaz, will be around 7,000 square feet. It will have five treatment rooms, along with a sauna, cold plunge, relaxation area, and more.

The opening of this resort has been majorly delayed. It was initially announced in 2018 with a 2021 opening, but the timeline slipped by six years, presumably due to a combination of the pandemic, plus… well, how hotel construction projects often work out. Hopefully there are no additional delays beyond the current planned spring 2027 opening.

With the Andaz Turks & Caicos at Grace Bay bookable, what are rates like? For those redeeming points, this is a Category 8 World of Hyatt property, meaning a free night redemption in a standard room costs 35,000-75,000 points per night.

World of Hyatt’s new award chart sure makes top end redemptions expensive, unfortunately! As of now the hotel is primarily bookable between April and November of 2027, so this doesn’t really cover peak season. For most dates, I currently see rates of either 35,000 points, 45,000 points, or 55,000 points per night. So value here is highly dependent on which of those rates you can find.

When it comes to cash rates, those currently start at around $900-1,300 per night, and that depends on when you’re staying. That’s inclusive of the service charge, but exclusive of the taxes.

If you are looking to book a cash stay here, I’d recommend doing so through the Hyatt Privé program, which offers extra perks like room upgrades, complimentary breakfast, and a hotel credit.

I suppose good options on Grace Bay are limited, and this hotel is boutique. But at these rates, they better offer something significantly better than the typical Andaz experience, in my opinion.

Turks & Caicos is absolutely beautiful, and it’s an easy getaway from the United States, given how close it is to Florida. Historically, the country hasn’t had that many points hotels, though that’s slowly starting to change.

Several years back, we saw the opening of the Ritz-Carlton Turks & Caicos. It has an amazing location on Grace Bay and the grounds of the property are beautiful, but it otherwise doesn’t feel very luxurious, and lacks personality.

So it’ll be nice to have another points property, and I look forward to learning more about the Andaz. Maybe I’m overly optimistic, but I think the Andaz might just end up offering a better experience than the Ritz-Carlton, at least based on the design renderings, and also the more boutique scale of the property. Andaz really is quite an inconsistent brand.

I of course should acknowledge that many people are understandably frustrated by the way that Grace Bay has developed over the years, given all the huge concrete towers that have taken shape along the beach. It has definitely lost its charm a bit, though the beach is still gorgeous.

Even beyond Grace Bay, we’re seeing some other great new options in Turks & Caicos. In 2025, we saw the opening of Salterra Turks & Caicos, a Marriott Luxury Collection property. This is great for those who want a bit more secluded of a trip, since South Caicos Island is a bit less crowded than the area around Providenciales. This is also where Sailrock Resort is located, which is an independent hotel affiliated with Small Luxury Hotels of the World (SLH).

There’s also a Waldorf Astoria Turks & Caicos planned for a 2028 opening, located on Dellis Cay, a nearby island that’s not as developed, which can be reached by a 25-minute boat transfer from Providenciales. That should also be a great option, especially with how the Waldorf Astoria portfolio is developing. However, don’t count on that timeline sticking either.

The Andaz Turks & Caicos is accepting reservations for stays as of April 2027, and it will be located on the famous Grace Bay. The property will have just 59 hotel rooms, in addition to residences, so I like how it’s on a smaller scale than some other properties.

This should be a very nice addition to the Caribbean points hotel market. Hopefully we don’t see any additional delays with the opening…

What do you make of the upcoming Andaz Turks & Caicos?

#6235. Oneworld Explains The Money Behind Your Lounge Access—And Why Credit Cards Help Decide Where Airlines Fly

Historically, if I used Royal Jordanian status to enter an American Airlines lounge while flying American, Royal Jordanian didn’t get a bill. American was carrying me and bore the lounge cost. In a new interview, oneworld’s commercial chief describes a payment model that sounds like that arrangement may still apply, despite reporting that says the rules changed. Who pays for your lounge visit helps explain why airline alliances are so difficult to run. The airline that gives you status, the one selling you a ticket, and the one providing your benefits can all be different. Each wants the customer and the revenue, and they have to agree on who picks up the costs. Roger Blackburn, oneworld’s Vice President of Commercial and Loyalty, and Gilbert Ott, its Director of Loyalty (and former blogger of God Save the Points), talk about how this works in an unusually candid interview. It’s essentially herding cats, with airlines that compete for the same customers promising to take care of each other’s passengers. Blackburn explains that a lounge hosting another airline’s passenger gets paid by: …the airline who’s … lifting that customer out of the station. At least that’s how our model works. One Mile at a Time has said its understanding is that this changed, and that the program providing status now pays when status is the reason someone gets in. This affects the economics of status matches, for instance. An airline offering status to someone who mostly flies its partners has a very different cost calculation if it’s getting a bill for every lounge visit. The lack of billing was also a limiting factor on offering status matches (confined to a formula relative to the total size of the elite pool). Blackburn describes the lounge operator as delighted to have another airline’s passenger because they’re getting paid. That true when there are empty seats. When the lounge is full, another paid visit can make the experience worse for the airline’s own customers. I’ve written about American’s lounge visits growing several times as fast as its passenger traffic. Better lounges encourage more people to use them, and to stay longer. Improving the product creates demand for more space. That’s also why Blackburn’s explanation of where oneworld builds its own lounges is helpful. They want airports served by enough member airlines to keep a lounge busy across the day. One airline might struggle to justify the rent and staffing for a single daily departure. Several airlines with departures at different times can share a better facility. Delhi and Mumbai come up in the conversation, and Blackburn hopes to have more lounge news “fairly soon.” The banks competing for that space also help pay for the airlines’ products. Ott argues that credit card and loyalty revenue supports better lounges, seats, food and inflight connectivity. He’s largely right, and the case goes further: credit cards support more flights. An airline becomes more attractive to cardmembers when it flies where they need to go. It also needs destinations they want to redeem their miles for. Delta has explicitly connected its growth in Austin and Raleigh with acquiring American Express card customers. A flight that looks weak based only on ticket revenue might make sense once you count the card spending it helps generate. As I discussed in my recent piece on Scott Kirby and credit card economics, a customer might choose an airline’s card because its Chicago schedule works for their business travel, then redeem the miles for Hawaii. Assign all the card revenue to Hawaii and you can end up cutting the flights that made someone want your card in the first place. A better seat and lounge help sell that relationship, too. And an alliance makes the card more useful by offering places to spend miles that the airline doesn’t fly to itself. Of course airlines can manage this badly. Sell more miles while planes are full, without making enough desirable award seats available, and customers wind up with growing balances they struggle to use. Sell more lounge access without adding enough capacity and the customer gets a line at the door. The alliance has to get its members to participate in making those benefits valuable. Asked whether oneworld should set minimum protections around changes to earning, status qualification and award availability, Ott describes the programs as largely sovereign and emphasizes a spirit of cooperation. Asked how much say the alliance has over the number of award seats a member releases, he calls it a collaborative process. I’d put it a different way: an alliance trying to influence airlines is pushing on a string. It’s the problem I’ve written about with airlines holding back their best awards from partners. They want to offer their members access to everyone else’s seats. But making their own best seats available can benefit another airline’s credit card business, while keeping those seats for their own members can help sell their own miles. Ott makes the case that a redemption can introduce someone to an airline and turn them into a valuable customer. That’s true as far as it goes, but those seats have an opportunity cost and getting the airline with the seat to value that speculative future business enough to release it (for a foreign customer who might not travel with them often and probably won’t take their credit card) can be a challenge. So can getting the partner buying the award seat to pay enough to make that worthwhile. Blackburn says oneworld is improving how quickly miles reach accounts following a flight across the alliance, with everyone expected on a new standard by the end of the year. He also says oneworld’s earlier artificial intelligence round the world booking assistant is gone, despite earlier claims of a fivefold increase in booking conversions. The interview returns to the oneworld Loyalty Summit in September, where I spoke about how artificial intelligence gives customers better tools to choose rewards programs. (The summit photo below is courtesy of oneworld.) Ott mentions verifying elite status without relying on screenshots that someone can easily manipulate. I saw a presentation at the summit for a product that was basically Plaid for airline status: the customer logged into their existing airline account to demonstrate their status to another company. I questioned whether airlines would allow that access to their systems. #6234. JetBlue Leads The Industry In Raising Checked Bag Fees… Again!

For whatever reason, JetBlue tends to be the industry leader when it comes to raising checked bag fees, and competitors tend to follow. Earlier this year, JetBlue was the first major US carrier to raise checked bag fees, and now the airline is raising checked bag fees again…

Effective immediately (for tickets purchased as of November 3, 2026), JetBlue has increased checked bag fees. JetBlue has a rather complicated fee structure for checked bags, with both off-peak and peak pricing, plus different pricing based on whether you pay for the bag 24 hours or more in advance.

Below is a chart with JetBlue’s new checked bag fees.

As you can see, an off-peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $50-60 (depending on whether you pay in advance), while a peak first checked bag on a domestic flight will now cost you $55-70 (depending on whether you pay in advance). For context, below are the dates that are considered peak for the purposes of bag fees.

It goes without saying that paying $50-70 for a first checked bag is a pretty substantial cost, especially when you consider how little checked bags used to cost. On a one-way, you’re looking at $100-140. For a family of four, you’d be looking at $400-560.

When JetBlue raised checked bag fees earlier this year, the airline released a statement claiming it was increasing checked bag fees to be “more competitive,” and that “while we recognize that fee increases are never ideal, we take careful consideration to ensure these changes are implemented only when necessary.” I imagine this time around, the logic is much of the same.

The simple reality is that oil prices are way up. Airlines have actually done a solid job of being able to make fare increases stick. But that’s not enough to fully offset the increase in the cost of jet fuel.

JetBlue is in a rough financial spot, and it hasn’t turned a profit since before the pandemic. The airline is hoping to turn an operating profit in 2027, though that strikes me as being particularly optimistic. So the logic for raising checked bags is threefold:

JetBlue has just increased checked bag fees once again, and you’ll now pay $50-70 for a first checked bag on a domestic flight. This is JetBlue’s second price increase on checked bags so far this year. When airlines are trying to increase revenue, checked bag fees are often low hanging fruit.

When competitors match, it also becomes something that’s unavoidable for consumers, other than getting a credit card… which also has upside for the airline! I’d be shocked if other airlines don’t match this move from JetBlue.

What do you make of JetBlue increasing checked bag fees?

#6233. American Airlines Passenger Stuck Overnight Couldn’t Get A Hotel Voucher—They Got A Credit Card Pitch Instead

An American Airlines passenger says they couldn’t get a hotel voucher during a flight delay. The chat agent did, however, have something else ready: a pitch to open a Citi credit card, spend $2,500, and earn 50,000 miles. That’s not even as good as the standard offer! American’s stated purpose is “To Care for People on Life’s Journey.” That journey includes a sales presentation while you’re trying to figure out where to sleep. The passenger shared a screenshot of the exchange. It begins with the agent asking, “Does any of that work for you?” Then comes a lengthy offer for the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select Mastercard: the initial bonus, free checked bags, double miles at restaurants and gas stations, and a request for permission to send a one-time email with more information. American Airlines offered me a credit card deal during a conversation about a delayed flight and their inability to provide a hotel voucher from mildlyinfuriating Always be selling! Always be closing! It’s Glengarry Glen Ross, and the passenger asking for help is the lead. American Pays Agents To Make These Pitches In May 2023, I reported that American’s reservations agents would switch from pitching Avis rental cars to Citi credit cards. At the time, I argued that agents should judge whether the conversation had gone well enough for a customer to be receptive. American’s AAdvantage Cash support materials explain why an agent might make the ask either way: Contact center and Premium Guest Services representatives earn at least $50 for each approved application carrying their referral code. That rises to $100 as they move through annual sales tiers. There are also $100, $300, and $500 bonuses for reaching Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. They earn elite status like we do. There’s also a separate guide to pitching cards during chats, complete with prescribed transitions from talking about travel benefits to offering the card. American Already Knows When To Stop Selling I’ve written for years about credit card announcements that interrupt sleep on early morning flights. As Kevin Williamson once put it, [T]here is the Clockwork Orange sensation of being literally strapped into a seat while someone screams corporate banalities at you on a loudspeaker fifteen inches from your head… It is a “limited-time” offer in the sense that the sun eventually will run out of gas and become a dying star, first engulfing the Earth in fire and then leaving the wreck of the solar system a sterile plane of interstellar cold and utter silence, which will be interrupted only by some addled flight attendant screeching about the limited-time Barclays card offer. The airline’s guidelines at least suggest: Use the approved script, which should take about a minute. Make the announcement only once per flight segment, at cruise before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. Skip late night and redeye flights. Refrain from offering the card or making announcements during delays, cancellations, diversions, and other events affecting the customer experience. Meanwhile, the pressure to sell keeps growing. On October 15, the flight attendants union objected to American inserting a 15-minute card-sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. Selling remains voluntary, but management made the training required and offered a $25 qualification reward. They Have A Sales Script For Your Bag Fee, Too American’s airport agent talking points for “Real Time Benefits” identify two moments to pitch: when a customer is about to pay a checked bag fee, and when they’re worried there won’t be overhead bin space for their carry-on. For most instantly approved applicants, the card’s first checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding can apply to the trip a passenger is already taking. The airline says the boarding group can take roughly seven minutes to update on a digital boarding pass. If the customer has already prepaid for bags, agents are told to shift the pitch to the miles, boarding, and free bags on a future eligible trip. I’ve even proposed plastering aircraft lavatories with credit card ads if attaching revenue to that space would persuade American to give us larger bathrooms since the space becomes monetized rather than deadweight loss. The inflight sales operation has instructions for distributing the commissions fairly among participating flight attendants. Brochures are prefilled with employee numbers, then stacked in a 1–2–3–3–2–1 sequence when three crew members participate. They’ve worked out whose referral code the next passenger gets. A Few Applications Don’t Prove This Is A Good Idea Maybe the number of applications generated from unhappy customers isn’t zero. The agent already has their attention, the sales text is ready to paste, and a small number of approvals can produce real money. But a positive response rate doesn’t establish that the pitch was worth making. You have to count the customers you make angrier, the business they take elsewhere, and whether someone who applies will actually keep and use the card. As I covered in looking at American’s Citi economics, their ambitions depend on acquiring customers, retaining them, and getting their spending. American’s deal announcement projected annual payments approaching $10 billion. They’ve finally come to realize that it matters whether customers like the airline enough to carry it in their wallet. In August, I covered their push for friendlier inflight service to increase card applications. Taking care of passengers makes them more receptive to the pitch. A customer service chat that hasn’t resolved the passenger’s hotel problem starts with.. not that. The passenger shared a screenshot of the exchange. It begins with the agent asking, “Does any of that work for you?” Then comes a lengthy offer for the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select Mastercard: the initial bonus, free checked bags, double miles at restaurants and gas stations, and a request for permission to send a one-time email with more information.

American Airlines offered me a credit card deal during a conversation about a delayed flight and their inability to provide a hotel voucher from mildlyinfuriating

Always be selling! Always be closing! It’s Glengarry Glen Ross, and the passenger asking for help is the lead.

In May 2023, I reported that American’s reservations agents would switch from pitching Avis rental cars to Citi credit cards. At the time, I argued that agents should judge whether the conversation had gone well enough for a customer to be receptive. American’s AAdvantage Cash support materials explain why an agent might make the ask either way: Contact center and Premium Guest Services representatives earn at least $50 for each approved application carrying their referral code. That rises to $100 as they move through annual sales tiers. There are also $100, $300, and $500 bonuses for reaching Gold, Platinum, and Diamond. They earn elite status like we do. There’s also a separate guide to pitching cards during chats, complete with prescribed transitions from talking about travel benefits to offering the card. American Already Knows When To Stop Selling I’ve written for years about credit card announcements that interrupt sleep on early morning flights. As Kevin Williamson once put it, [T]here is the Clockwork Orange sensation of being literally strapped into a seat while someone screams corporate banalities at you on a loudspeaker fifteen inches from your head… It is a “limited-time” offer in the sense that the sun eventually will run out of gas and become a dying star, first engulfing the Earth in fire and then leaving the wreck of the solar system a sterile plane of interstellar cold and utter silence, which will be interrupted only by some addled flight attendant screeching about the limited-time Barclays card offer. The airline’s guidelines at least suggest: Use the approved script, which should take about a minute. Make the announcement only once per flight segment, at cruise before descent, between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. Skip late night and redeye flights. Refrain from offering the card or making announcements during delays, cancellations, diversions, and other events affecting the customer experience. Meanwhile, the pressure to sell keeps growing. On October 15, the flight attendants union objected to American inserting a 15-minute card-sales module into mandatory fourth quarter training. Selling remains voluntary, but management made the training required and offered a $25 qualification reward. They Have A Sales Script For Your Bag Fee, Too American’s airport agent talking points for “Real Time Benefits” identify two moments to pitch: when a customer is about to pay a checked bag fee, and when they’re worried there won’t be overhead bin space for their carry-on. For most instantly approved applicants, the card’s first checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding can apply to the trip a passenger is already taking. The airline says the boarding group can take roughly seven minutes to update on a digital boarding pass. If the customer has already prepaid for bags, agents are told to shift the pitch to the miles, boarding, and free bags on a future eligible trip. I’ve even proposed plastering aircraft lavatories with credit card ads if attaching revenue to that space would persuade American to give us larger bathrooms since the space becomes monetized rather than deadweight loss. The inflight sales operation has instructions for distributing the commissions fairly among participating flight attendants. Brochures are prefilled with employee numbers, then stacked in a 1–2–3–3–2–1 sequence when three crew members participate. They’ve worked out whose referral code the next passenger gets. A Few Applications Don’t Prove This Is A Good Idea Maybe the number of applications generated from unhappy customers isn’t zero. The agent already has their attention, the sales text is ready to paste, and a small number of approvals can produce real money. But a positive response rate doesn’t establish that the pitch was worth making. You have to count the customers you make angrier, the business they take elsewhere, and whether someone who applies will actually keep and use the card. As I covered in looking at American’s Citi economics, their ambitions depend on acquiring customers, retaining them, and getting their spending. American’s deal announcement projected annual payments approaching $10 billion. They’ve finally come to realize that it matters whether customers like the airline enough to carry it in their wallet. In August, I covered their push for friendlier inflight service to increase card applications. Taking care of passengers makes them more receptive to the pitch. A customer service chat that hasn’t resolved the passenger’s hotel problem starts with.. not that. @Matt — For meaningful air passenger rights legislation… please consider EU261.

I flew on AA for the first time in 6+ years last month. I hadn’t heard CC pitches on any other airline in all that time.

For meaningful air passenger rights legislation

You’d get more done by parachuting teams of forensic accountants into every major airline.

Once again, if airlines are that dependent on sweet, sweet credit-card revenue, re-evaluating the entire business model is long overdue.

There are so many reasons not to fly AA. This one is so insidious that you want to throttle the messenger, but would wind up being arrested

@1990 – Follow the money, and the need for any additional rules will make themselves clear.

Worth knowing for next time. AA commits to a hotel for delays and cancellations that are its fault, so ask whether the cause is controllable. If it is, ask at the gate or the service desk rather than chat. If the agent can’t issue a voucher, book a cancellable airport hotel yourself straight away, keep the receipt and the delay code, then send it to customer relations. Weather is the catch, you’re on your own there. The airport hotels go first on a bad night, so speed matters more than price for the first room. FWIW that same airport hotel can price diff when searched from other countries since inventory and prices vary by market, free tools like Arbitrica check somewhat 200 countries for kinda the lowest price in the world. Then file the claim the next morning while the dits are fresh

@Denver Refugee — Oh, I’m all about ‘following the money,’ and if we actually did that, say, by attaching real financial penalties against airlines when they fail consumers… yeah, behavior would change. Fast. Overnight. We’re overdue for reforms. Gimme a US-261.

Earlier this year, JetBlue raised its checked bag fees and kicked off a wave of fee hikes across the industry. United followed. Then Delta, American and Southwest.

Seven months later, JetBlue is leading the fee-hiking charge again.

The carrier on Tuesday raised its bag fees for the second time in 2026.

Going forward, customers will pay at least $50 per bag. That’s a 28% jump from the lowest fee the airline previously charged its customers.

Passengers who don’t pre-pay for their bag will pay $60 for their first piece of checked luggage.

And because JetBlue uses a dynamic baggage-pricing system, flyers will pay even more for their checked baggage on peak travel days.

In a statement about the airline's second bag-fee hike this year, the carrier pointed to rising fuel and operating costs.

“This helps us keep our base fares competitive while giving customers the choice to pay for a checked bag only if they need one,” a spokesperson said.

Here’s how JetBlue’s bag fees will shake out, going forward.

These fees will apply to flights booked starting Nov. 3.

So if you had already purchased a JetBlue flight prior to Nov. 3 — including trips for the holidays — the previous fees would apply to your trip.

As noted above, JetBlue also raised the fees customers will pay for their second checked bag, too.

Here are the days where JetBlue's "peak" baggage fees will apply, through October 2027.

JetBlue does continue to offer free baggage perks as a benefit of certain cobranded credit cards. Plus, its Mosaic elite status members each get at least one free bag.

Customers flying in JetBlue’s premium Mint cabin are still entitled to their first bag free. The same goes for flyers who book the carrier’s new domestic first-class (BlueFirst) seats, which are set to debut on some flights next month.

As JetBlue raises its baggage fees, the biggest question for consumers is how the rest of the airline industry respond.

If history is any indication, we’re about to see another wave of fee hikes across the industry.

After JetBlue raised its bag fees in late March, it took only weeks for nearly every major U.S. carrier to follow with their own fee hikes.

This would be the latest case of sticker shock for travelers, who are simultaneously battling surging fares.

Even budget airline Frontier last week reported customers had paid 71% more in fares over the prior quarter.

All of this comes as airlines have had to contend with sky-high jet fuel costs in 2026 — which they’ve aggressively passed onto customers.

But while jet fuel costs may eventually fall, it’s unlikely flyers will see any future relief when it comes to baggage fees — typically, once those go up, they don’t come back down.

While JetBlue has raised its baggage fees, it is worth noting that passengers do have freedom to bring a full-size carry-on bag on JetBlue flights, regardless of the fare type. The airline no longer bars its Blue Basic (basic economy) passengers from using the overhead bins.

Of course, the belongings packed in any carry-on bag must meet the Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy.

#6231. Limited Time: Citi AAdvantage Business Card 75K Bonus Miles Offer (Double Dip Loyalty Points!)

The Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® is American’s primary co-branded business credit card. We’ve just seen an excellent new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the card, which is in line with the highest ever offer that we’ve seen on the card.

That makes this the ideal time to apply. Not only that, but this is a card that many people will want, given that it’s my favorite American card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can basically double dip Loyalty Points.

Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard®

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card currently has a limited time welcome offer of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a highest-ever offer, in line with the best bonuses I recall seeing on the card.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I value AAdvantage miles at 1.5 cents each, so to me the bonus is worth $1,125. There are some incredible uses of American AAdvantage miles, including for travel on some world class partner airlines.

Also keep in mind that credit card spending will qualify for Loyalty Points (helping you earn elite status, including Gold, Platinum, Platinum Pro, or Executive Platinum), though the welcome bonus as such won’t. Upon completing minimum spending, you’d earn a minimum of 5,000 Loyalty Points. As I’ll explain below, you can even double dip the Loyalty Points you earn.

If you’re interested in applying for the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, the typical Citi credit card application restrictions apply, including that you can be approved for at most one Citi card every eight days, and at most two Citi cards every 65 days.

On top of that, the bonus isn’t available to those who have received a new account bonus on this exact card in the past 48 months. Eligibility is unrelated to having any other American Airlines credit cards.

If you’re concerned about Chase’s 5/24 rule, note that applying for a Citi business card generally won’t count toward that limit. I should also mention that at least anecdotally, this card seems to be quite easy to get approved for.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card has an annual fee that’s waived for the first year, so you can “try” the card before you have to pay a fee. While the fee after that is technically still $99, it’s increasing to $150 as of January 24, 2027, so that’s what you’d pay on account renewal.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card offers a variety of valuable perks, including:

Above I mentioned how the Citi AAdvantage Business Card is the best card for earning AAdvantage elite status. The reason is because through December 31, 2028, the card essentially lets you double dip Loyalty Points. If you add an authorized user, their spending will earn 1x Loyalty Points per dollar spent for both their own account, and for the primary cardmember’s account. So this is a way to essentially get two-for-one elite status qualification, which is awesome.

With the annual fee increasing as of January 2027, the card will also pick up several valuable new perks, including the following:

Read a detailed review of the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus of 75,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 within the first five months. This is a great offer on a valuable card that even has its annual fee waived for the first year.

This is also my favorite card for earning AAdvantage elite status, since you can essentially earn Loyalty Points for two members at once. Authorized user spending earns Loyalty Points for the authorized user’s AAdvantage account, and also for the primary cardmember’s AAdvantage account.

Anyone plan to pick up the Citi AAdvantage Business Card with 75K miles?

The Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® is the single best card for earning airline status. And for a limited time, earn 75,000 American Airlines AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $5,000 in purchases within the first 5 months of account opening. [See rates and fees]

The card’s $99 annual fee is waived for the first year, but even if it weren’t the initial bonus offer would be compelling. (The card’s annual fee will be increasing to $150 for existing cardmembers January 24, 2027. That won’t affect those approved for the card now until card renewal at the conclusion of the first year, because the annual fee is $0 for the first 12 months.)

I have the card. I’m keeping it because it allows you to have the same purchases earn credit towards status for two people. For instance,

$125,000 in eligible spending on an employee card can produce 125,000 Loyalty Points for the employee and another 125,000 Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. That’s enough for both to earn Platinum Pro status. On an American Airlines personal card, only one person would earn this status. It’s leverage no other airline’s card offers. Put spending on an employee card, and both that individual and the primary cardholder earns status credit from the same spending. American lists this as valid through December 31, 2028 but that doesn’t mean it won’t be extended. American’s business card earns redeemable miles that go into the company’s AAdvantage Business account, which are also transferable to individual AAdvantage accounts and you can choose where they go later. I have the recently-refreshed Citi Executive card that now awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualifying year. Those thresholds are triggered by Loyalty Points earned across your AAdvantage account, and doesn’t require spending a single dollar on the Executive card itself. I’m a primary Citi Executive card holder. If I get one for my wife, then $105,000 on her business employee card would produce 105,000 Loyalty Points for each of us plus 20,000 in Executive card bonuses apiece. $105,000 spend becomes enough for two Platinum Pro and oneworld emerald statuses (without loyalty points from any other source, including Citi Globe’s ‘flight streak’ bonus). The card earns: 3 miles per dollar on eligible bookings through AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars. 2 miles per dollar in one chosen category: U.S. shipping, office supply stores, or U.S. advertising. And it offers a $100 inflight credit which covers food, beverages and Wi-Fi. Spend $30,000 during your cardmembership year and renew, and you can earn a certificate for a companion’s eligible domestic Main Cabin roundtrip for $99 plus taxes and fees. The card also receives first checked bag free on eligible domestic itineraries and preferred boarding for the primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation, 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages, and no foreign transaction fees. #6229. Air Tahiti Nui Will Offer Free Starlink Wi-Fi On Its Boeing 787s As Of 2027

Air Tahiti Nui has just announced a massive upgrade to its inflight connectivity, as the airline will be rolling out free Starlink Wi-Fi across its (small) fleet in 2027.

Air Tahiti Nui has revealed that it plans to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its entire fleet, which consists of four Boeing 787-9s. The airline plans to offer this service for free to passengers in all travel classes.

Starlink will be introduced in 2027, though no timeline beyond that is known yet, so it could be early or late in the year. Presumably once installation starts, it’ll be completed very quickly — four planes could easily be fitted with Starlink in a single week.

Air Tahiti Nui operates some very long flights — including from Papeete (PPT) to Paris (CDG) via Los Angeles (LAX) so having fast and free connectivity is super valuable. While so many airlines market their Wi-Fi as being high speed, Starlink is the only product currently in service where you can consistently stream videos, etc.

Currently, Air Tahiti Nui’s Dreamliners are equipped with Panasonic Wi-Fi, which actually has relatively decent speeds. The catch is that Air Tahiti Nui chooses to have insanely high pricing based primarily on data usage, rather than just offering a full flight pass for a fixed amount.

Below is Air Tahiti Nui’s current pricing chart for Wi-Fi… could they make this any more complicated? $28 for 100 MB of data is absurd, and $98 for unlimited data is even more ridiculous.

This kind of pricing just strikes me as being so stupid. All you end up doing is frustrating passengers, and I also have to imagine this isn’t actually the system that maximizes usage. It’s weird to have a provider with speeds that are actually semi-usable (Panasonic is better than OnAir), and to then do this with it.

So anyway, Starlink will simply be a massive upgrade for Air Tahiti Nui in every way. Speaking of which, I’d sure love to return to French Polynesia at some point (and fly that all-business class Air Tahiti turboprop, while I’m at it).

In 2027, Air Tahiti Nui intends to install Starlink Wi-Fi on its fleet of four Dreamliners. It remains to be seen exactly when in 2027 it’ll happen, but this represents a huge upgrade to the passenger experience. The airline currently offers Panasonic Wi-Fi with awful data-based pricing (or an unlimited package that will run you close to $100).

What do you make of Air Tahiti Nui introducing Starlink?

#6228. GOP senator's 30-year reign ends as 5th-generation logger pulls off stunning upset

Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson takes aim at longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins' seniority argument, charging that 'we're losing money.' Collins returns fire, saying the state will lose out on funding if Jackson is elected.

Fifth-generation logger Troy Jackson has pulled off a major upset in Maine, defeating incumbent Republican Sen. Susan Collins and giving the Democratic Party a major boost in the battle for the U.S. Senate, the Fox News Decision Desk projects.

Jackson's victory will end Collins’ nearly three-decade career in the Senate.

"Maine, I owe you everything," Jackson wrote on X. "I’m ready to get to work for Mainers in the U.S. Senate, and I promise you this: I’ll never forget where I came from or who I’m fighting for."

The win gives Democrats a major pickup in one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm elections. The Maine contest was viewed as a critical test of whether Democrats could defeat a Republican incumbent in a state that has shifted increasingly toward the party in recent presidential elections.

The result also could have major implications for control of the Senate.

SCHUMER WARNS OF REPUBLICAN ADVANTAGE THAT COULD CHANGE THE BATTLE FOR SENATE CONTROL

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, left, is on a glide path to replace former candidate Graham Platner as the Democratic Party's Senate nominee in Maine and face off in the midterm elections against longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins. (Ryan Murphy/Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I'm proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years," Collins wrote in conceding the race to her Democratic challenger.

"I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition."

Jackson previously served as president of the Maine Senate and represented parts of Aroostook County in the state Legislature. He campaigned as a working-class Democrat and labor advocate who would challenge both Washington’s political establishment and wealthy interests after he replaced disgraced Senate nominee Graham Platner on the ballot.

Platner dropped out of the race in July amid allegations of sexual assault, which prompted a vote within the Maine Democratic Party to install Jackson.

Jackson's campaign was nearly knocked off its tracks early on when it was revealed his longtime partner and mother of his two children is also his second cousin — the two share great-grandparents, according to reports. But that scandal wasn't enough to stop him from toppling the political institution that is Senator Collins.

COLLINS INSISTS SOCIALIST RIVAL WON'T BEAT HER AS MAINE'S MONEY MACHINE: 'YOU'LL LOSE BIG TIME'

Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate Troy Jackson shakes hands with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, before their debate at the Gracie Theatre in Bangor, Maine on Oct. 15, 2026. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

Collins, who was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996, was seeking a sixth term. She is Maine’s longest-serving member of Congress and chaired the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee, a position that gave her significant influence over federal spending and funding for Maine projects.

Collins, one of the more moderate Republicans in the Senate, built her latest re-election campaign around her reputation for independence and bipartisan dealmaking. She highlighted her work on infrastructure, veterans’ issues, rural communities and federal assistance for Maine residents while arguing that her seniority and committee position gave the state an advantage in Washington.

The race was shaped by Collins’ complicated relationship with President Donald Trump and the Republican Party. Democrats criticized Collins over her votes for Trump-backed policies and her vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, arguing that her reputation as a moderate no longer matched her voting record.

Then-Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Graham Platner speaks to voters at a town hall at the Elks Lodge 188 on June 7, 2026, in Portland, Maine. (Laura Brett/Getty Images)

Collins countered by pointing to the times she opposed Trump and Senate Republicans. She emphasized her willingness to break with her party and argued that Maine voters valued her independence more than party loyalty.

"Troy and Chuck Schumer and their allies run ads saying that I'm somehow a puppet of the president. Believe me, that would come as a huge surprise to President Trump," the senator said in an interview last month with Fox News Digital.

Former Democratic Sen. Joe Manchin campaigned with Collins in the closing weeks of the race, helping her make the case that she was a bipartisan senator who could work with lawmakers from both parties.

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee, talks with supporters at a campaign event in Brunswick, Maine on Oct. 28, 2026. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Jackson’s victory marks a significant political shift in Maine and ends Collins’ run as one of the Republican Party’s most durable statewide candidates. Collins won re-election by nearly nine percentage points in 2020, but Democrats entered the 2026 contest with advantages driven by the state’s increasingly Democratic electorate and opposition to the Trump administration.

Jackson will enter the Senate as a former state legislative leader with strong ties to organized labor and rural Maine. His election is likely to make him a prominent voice on economic issues as Democrats seek to appeal to working-class voters across the country.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#6226. JetBlue Raises Bag Fees Again—One Checked Bag Can Cost $140 Roundtrip, Other Airlines Likely To Follow

JetBlue has raised checked bag fees again. Your first bag now costs at least $50 each way on domestic flights, and as much as $70 if you pay within 24 hours of departure on a peak travel date. That’s $140 roundtrip for one bag. They already raised bag fees earlier this year. And JetBlue has repeatedly gone first with these increases, then other airlines follow. So even if you don’t fly JetBlue, their tests of how much more passengers will pay can wind up costing you. A First Bag Starts At $50. A Second Reaches $85. The new pricing applies to bookings made November 3 onward. Here’s the new domestic schedule, per bag, each way: Checked bag Paid more than 24 hours ahead Paid within 24 hours First bag, off-peak $50 $60 First bag, peak $55 $70 Second bag, off-peak $70 $75 Second bag, peak $75 $85 Peak pricing is November 19–30, December 17–January 18, and May 20–September 8 next summer. A family of four checking one bag each, without a waiver, pays $440 roundtrip on peak dates even when they pay early. Wait until check-in and it’s $560. On transatlantic Main Base and EvenMore Base fares, the first bag is $80 off-peak or $90 peak when prepaid, rising to $90 or $100 within 24 hours. Standard Main and EvenMore transatlantic fares still include a first bag. Mosaic 1 elite status includes one checked bag and Mosaic 2–4 include two. JetBlue Plus and Premier cardholders have a first checked bag benefit. Those exemptions become a pitch for their credit card since things are worse for everyone else. And while they give you a discount for paying in advance, bag fees are refundable only when the entire booking is canceled before departure. If you pay for an extra bag you don’t wind up checking, you’re out of luck. By putting fear of high prices in passengers, they may generate revenue for services the customer winds up not ever needing and using. JetBlue Keeps Leading The Industry Toward Higher Bag Fees When I covered JetBlue’s increase in March, their cheapest first bag went from $35 to $39. The peak advance price rose to $49. Today’s $50 minimum is 28% higher than that March minimum, and 43% higher than the $35 price before it. In 2018, JetBlue led the move to a $30 first checked bag. United followed that same week. In January 2020, JetBlue went to $35 unless you prepaid. United announced its matching move the next month. In 2024, JetBlue added peak and off-peak baggage pricing, after already raising fees earlier that year. This spring, JetBlue raised fees in late March. United announced another increase days later. JetBlue isn’t the consumer-first airline anymore. When they introduced bag fees in 2015, the first bag was $20 online or at a kiosk, $25 at the counter. They defended their direction by pointing to how much worse other airlines were, declaring: The world is going in a very dramatic direction toward more and more commoditization. That’s not where we’re going. Now they’re leading in the race to the bottom. The Government Encourages This JetBlue tied the spring increase to rising operating costs. But an airline’s bag fee isn’t derived from the fuel needed to carry the bag. Fares and fees are set according to what airlines think customers will pay, subject to competition. Higher bag fees let JetBlue raise the cost of a trip while leaving the advertised airfare alone. They also make it harder to compare the total price across airlines. And the government rewards them for doing it. Domestic air transportation is generally subject to a 7.5% federal excise tax. Separate baggage fees are excluded from that tax. Every dollar an airline moves out of fares and into fees saves them 7.5 cents, even if the total price remains the same. I’ve made this point through previous rounds of JetBlue increases: anyone serious about pushing back on bag fees should start with the tax preference that encourages airlines to move money out of fares and into baggage charges. (HT: Enilria) Topics on this pageAirline IndustryJetBlueUnited Airlines+1 more More From View from the Wing

#6225. Flying Blue Delays SAF & Donation XP Changes Until December 2026

One unique aspect of the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program has long been how environmental contributions have contributed toward elite status, whether through the purchase of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), or through mileage donations to environmental causes.

A couple of days ago I covered how seemingly overnight, the Flying Blue program drastically decreased status qualification through these methods, requiring 50% larger contributions to earn the same number of XPs (experience points, the method by which one earns status). There’s now an update, and I’m pleased to see the way this is being handled.

Flying Blue has announced that it’s delaying the changes it’s making to the ability to earn XPs through SAF and mileage donations, and this will now be implemented as of December 1, 2026. Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, shared the following with me:

On Monday, we updated how many XP you earn on Sustainable Aviation Fuel and charitable contributions. We didn’t handle the rollout well, and the new rate went live with unclear messaging and without notice. While this affects a small share of our members, we recognize for those members it matters a great deal.

The update was part of a continuous review of our elite tiers. We want status to stay balanced across every way you earn XP, in the air and on the ground, so that we can keep delivering the benefits and service you expect.

For now, we’re pressing pause. From tomorrow (4 November), SAF and charitable contributions will earn XP at the previous rate, and any contribution made since 2 November will be credited at the prior rate as well. The new rate of €15 per XP begins on 1 December 2026; no program in the market will recognize SAF contributions more generously than Flying Blue, including on award tickets.

We want Flying Blue to be a program you build your life around. Many of you put a lot of care into planning your flights and status qualification, and we understand your need to have time to make adjustments.

And to everyone who told us why this matters to you: thank you for caring this much about Flying Blue.

I am happy to see how Flying Blue leadership is handling this situation. Let me share my take on this situation, broadly.

I don’t necessarily think Flying Blue had to make some big, public announcement about the change in advance. After all, this isn’t an official part of the program, and there has really never been any member communication about these opportunities.

I think what was frustrating is that the change was implemented before the website was even updated. So you had the higher pricing already showing, while the page about SAF and mileage donations still reflected the old cost, leaving many people wondering if the change was a glitch or intentional.

At a minimum, I think it’s appropriate to update the webpage before the changes go live, and ideally even give a little notice on the page dedicated to this, just so members aren’t caught off guard.

When it comes to the change as such, Flying Blue does indeed have the most generous opportunities to qualify for elite status through these types of contributions. Selfishly I love this option, but it’s not like members are “entitled” to a certain rate of qualification through this method, since there’s not actually any objectively “fair” way to reward elite qualification for contributions.

So for Flying Blue, it’s presumably about balancing environmental goals with elite ranks. I know with the 50% price hike, I’ll be much less likely to buy SAF, and that’s fine.

As of December 1, 2026, the Air France-KLM Flying Blue program will be decreasing the number of XPs that members earn for contributing toward sustainable aviation fuel and environmental causes. This was initially supposed to be implemented a couple of days ago, but members were caught off guard, so I appreciate that the implementation of this has been delayed.

If nothing else, that goes to show there's consistency in how the programme is run regardless of which manager's responsible for it.

Didn't affect me, personally, but at least they're trying to better address the lack of notice. Will this slight delay make a meaningful difference for those of you this did impact?

#6223. Transfer Citi ThankYou Points To Turkish Miles&Smiles With 40% Bonus: Worth It?

At the moment, it’s possible to earn up to a 40% bonus when you transfer Citi ThankYou points to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, the bonus isn’t being offered on Citi’s end, but instead, is being offered on Turkish Airlines’ end.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from the Citi ThankYou program in the United States to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. However, there are some important terms to be aware of:

Ordinarily points transfer at a 1:1 ratio (in 1,000 point increments), while through this promotion you’d get 1,400 Miles&Smiles miles for every 1,000 Citi ThankYou points transferred, though only after the fact.

There are several great cards earning Citi ThankYou points, including the Citi Strata Premier® Card (learn more) and Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (learn more), and it’s easy to combine points between the cards.

Back in the day, the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles program offered incredible redemption values across the board, but that’s no longer really the case. At this point, I’d say the sweet spot with the Miles&Smiles program is if you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines specifically to or from Istanbul.

That’s because the Miles&Smiles program now charges per segment for awards on Turkish Airlines metal. You can find the cost of one-way saver awards below, just to give you a sense of pricing.

So as an example, a one-way business class award between the United States and Istanbul will cost you 65,000 miles. In other words, with a 40% transfer bonus, you’d be paying around 47,000 Citi ThankYou points for a business class award, which is a pretty great deal.

If you know what you’re doing and have specific redemption plans in mind, this could be a great deal. Just be sure you understand the complexities of the program, and read my guide to the Turkish Miles&Smiles program. Also keep in mind the Miles&Smiles expiration policy, which is that miles expire at the end of the third year after which they’re earned, regardless of activity.

The other big restriction is that the bonus miles will only post after the campaign is done, so you couldn’t transfer points and then immediately redeem all of them (including the bonus). The cap on 50,000 bonus miles is also limiting. But hey, if you value Turkish miles, this could definitely offer some value.

Between November 1 and November 30, 2026, it’s possible to receive a 40% bonus when you move points from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles. The catch is that the bonus miles only post after the end of the campaign, and you can only earn 50,000 bonus miles with this offer.

If you’re looking to travel on Turkish Airlines to or from Istanbul, there are some good deals to be had by taking advantage of this.

Do you plan on taking advantage of this transfer bonus from Citi ThankYou to Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles?
