Last week, a high-ranking set of Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish officials came to Tehran, where they met an Iranian delegation led by Mohsen Rezaei. Rezaei, former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), heads Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). The SNSC is the country’s top decision-making body and brings together leaders from the IRGC and conventional military, along with representatives of the supreme leader and elected officials. In this meeting, Rezaei was joined by President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

That these officials—representing Iran’s top security body, its president, and its foreign minister—all participated in the meeting suggests a degree of consensus across Iran’s political spectrum. In the past, many Iranian diplomatic efforts had been the sole prerogative of the foreign ministry, without buy-in from military and security institutions, which made their implementation difficult. This meeting, on the other hand, demonstrates that, across different centers of power, Iran’s political and military establishment is serious about diplomacy.

Last week, a high-ranking set of Saudi, Pakistani, and Turkish officials came to Tehran, where they met an Iranian delegation led by Mohsen Rezaei. Rezaei, former commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), heads Iran’s Supreme National Security Council (SNSC). The SNSC is the country’s top decision-making body and brings together leaders from the IRGC and conventional military, along with representatives of the supreme leader and elected officials. In this meeting, Rezaei was joined by President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

That these officials—representing Iran’s top security body, its president, and its foreign minister—all participated in the meeting suggests a degree of consensus across Iran’s political spectrum. In the past, many Iranian diplomatic efforts had been the sole prerogative of the foreign ministry, without buy-in from military and security institutions, which made their implementation difficult. This meeting, on the other hand, demonstrates that, across different centers of power, Iran’s political and military establishment is serious about diplomacy.

The seniority of the Iranians’ interlocutors also underscores the importance of these talks. Pakistan was represented by Field Marshal Asim Munir, the country’s de facto most influential political figure. Saudi Arabia sent Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, the younger brother and confidant of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, while Turkey sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin, a longtime close advisor to President Recep Tayyip Erdogan with extensive experience in regional diplomacy.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are also members of the Mecca defense pact, suggesting that Iran wants to play a greater role in the regional security architecture rather than acting outside of it. This is important, as Saudi Arabia in particular faces both continued attacks from Iran’s Houthi allies and risks becoming the target of IRGC strikes should the war break out again.

The meeting ended with a joint statement signed by Rezaei, Salman, Munir, and Kalin in which the four committed their countries to continued dialogue and regional “peace and security.” The statement was vague but signals that Iran does not want to immediately escalate and is instead open to having a productive relationship with its neighbors, some of whom it was targeting with missile and drone strikes just months earlier. This is supported by reports that the Iranian leadership responded positively to a letter sent last month by U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance to Rezaei, in which the former stressed the need for diplomacy.

But the meeting came on the heels of another significant development in the Iranian security landscape that signals that Iran is preparing to escalate if it must: the appointment of Mehrdad Akhlaghi as defense minister. His appointment indicates a shift in the defense establishment to a focus on offensive capabilities. Akhlaghi previously led the Shahid Bagheri Industrial Group (SBIG), where he worked on developing Iran’s ballistic missiles, particularly those that use solid-fuel propellants. Compared to liquid-fuel missiles, solid-fuel missiles are easier to store, require less maintenance, and are less vulnerable to detection. As much of the U.S.-Israel strategy during the war centered on neutralizing Iran’s missiles, the importance of these operationally advantageous missiles should war break out again will increase—a consideration that may have played a role in Akhlaghi’s appointment.

After the SBIG, Akhlaghi went up the Iranian military-industrial ladder. He led the Aerospace Industries Organization, which oversees the missile program as a whole. He then headed the Defense Industries Organization, which oversees the manufacturing of all Iranian military hardware, including drones, which were also key to Iran’s military operations in the Gulf during this year’s war. His appointment marks a shift from his predecessor, Aziz Nasirzadeh, who was a former fighter pilot and came from Iran’s conventional air force, rather than institutions associated with the IRGC and its weaponry. Nasirzadeh was killed during the Feb. 28 attacks and, since then, the defense ministry had been led in the interim by Majid Ebn-e-Reza.

The U.S. military faces “profound” long-term readiness concerns, one expert said.

Akhlaghi will be tasked with rapidly rebuilding Iranian military capabilities—mainly missiles and drones—that have been degraded by U.S. and Israeli attacks. This suggests that Iran is preparing, simply put, to pummel the Gulf countries if war breaks out again.

In a recent speech, Akhlaghi stated that “if [U.S. President Donald] Trump drops a single bomb, his forces are going to leave the region horizontally (i.e., in body bags).” That would require a significant campaign against the Gulf—precisely the type of escalation that Salman was likely seeking to prevent during his time in Tehran. Akhlaghi’s influence in Iran could extend beyond the defense ministry to the SNSC, where he can participate in deliberations and vote on matters concerning national defense.

An insistence on regional diplomacy while simultaneously appointing a defense minister whose primary responsibility revolves around rebuilding the capabilities designed to wreak havoc on the Gulf might seem contradictory. But these moves reveal Iran’s broader strategy of hedging, at the core of which is a simple reality: Iran does not seem to know what is coming next.

In this state of limbo, Iran is watching international developments for clues as to what may be in store. Israeli elections, for example, have been covered extensively in Iranian media. Conservative outlets close to the supreme leader’s office, for instance, have amplified reports that Gadi Eisenkot, unlike incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, is against regime change operations in Iran, as he has recognized that the Islamic Republic cannot be overthrown militarily. Eisenkot does not fully oppose military operations but instead believes that, should Israel attack Iran, it should target specific installations, such as nuclear facilities, rather than launch an all-out war.

Such reporting shows that, before the election, there was some cautious optimism in Iranian political circles: An Eisenkot-led government would be less willing to restart the war against Iran and might revert to smaller-scale sabotage operations that were common before the wars. From Tehran’s point of view, a change in Israeli leadership could also reduce the likelihood of renewed U.S. intervention, given Iran’s belief that Israel dragged the U.S. into the war.

Though Likud emerged as the party with the most votes, Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority, and Eisenkot has warned Netanyahu against conducting an attack in the absence of a majority—even going as far as to call on security officials to stand firm against the prime minister. Netanyahu will have a tough time forming a government, as he would need to coax members of Eisenkot’s bloc into defecting. But Eisenkot, whose party underperformed in the elections, will also not be able to form a government without the support of Arab parties, which he has previously expressed opposition to including in any coalition.

Iran is also watching the American midterm elections, which similarly provoke more questions than answers. Some Iranian media sources have relayed reports from U.S. outlets that a Democratic victory in the midterms could constrain Trump’s ability to sustain a prolonged military campaign against Iran. Yet even if Democrats win control of Congress, they will not take office until January, leaving Trump two months to act without facing the constraints of a Democrat-controlled legislature. Once his party is freed from electoral pressures and concerns over rising gas prices, he might capitalize on that window to resume military action—even as his vice president is attempting to pursue diplomacy.

This uncertainty lies at the heart of Iran’s strategic calculations. Iran wants to convince its neighbors that it can be a partner for peace, while rebuilding its capacity to wage war. Whether diplomacy succeeds—or even has a chance to succeed—will depend on several factors, including who comes to power in Israel and how Trump acts after the midterms. In the meantime, Tehran is hoping for the best but expecting the worst.

Ashkan Hashemipour is a D.Phil. candidate at the University of Oxford in modern Iranian history and politics.

#6074. Democrats flip House as Republicans confront ‘blue tsunami’

Democrats seized control of the House on Tuesday by safeguarding vulnerable incumbents and flipping districts in both battleground and deep-red terrain, delivering a sweeping repudiation of Donald Trump and Republicans that threatens to stall the president’s remaining agenda.

The Associated Press call came at 1:26 a.m. Eastern time Wednesday, hours after Democrats were projected to win a majority in the Senate, with a string of victories in deeply conservative states.

“The American people have spoken and made clear they’ve had enough of the extremism, enough of the corruption,’’ House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is poised to become the first Black speaker, told cheering supporters in Washington. “They want a Congress that’s going to deliver for the American people, and that is exactly what House Democrats will do.”

Recent polls had forecast a strong Democratic showing amid rising discontent with the president’s policies and economic anxiety driven by rising prices and the Iran war. But the magnitude of the Democratic majority surprised even the most optimistic Democratic partisans.

The “blue tsunami” marked an extraordinary turnaround for a party that suffered withering losses in 2024, when Trump returned to the White House and Republicans won a governing trifecta in Washington.

Republicans had hoped that a mid-decade redistricting push driven by Trump would help them keep their majority by flipping House seats in Texas, North Carolina, Florida and Ohio, among other states. Instead, many of those districts remained in Democrats’ hands.

Trump put himself front and center of the midterm campaign, imploring voters to “pretend that I’m on the ballot.” On Tuesday, he posted on social media that he “wasn’t on the ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

But in a later interview with CBS News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their rout. “My message is, congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country,” he said.

Among the night’s Democratic pickups were seats in rural and Republican-leaning districts. Farmer Jamie Ager defeated Republican state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom to flip a Western North Carolina seat that was left open after Republican Chuck Edwards announced his retirement after facing allegations of sexual harassment.

In Kentucky’s 6th District, Democrat Zach Dembo, a Navy veteran and former federal prosecutor, defeated former state Sen. Ralph Alvarado for an open seat anchored in Lexington.

Democrats also swept perennial battleground districts, flipping seats in states such as New Jersey, Colorado and Wisconsin. And in Pennsylvania, Democrats were projected to flip all four seats they were targeting, including the Philadelphia-area district of GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.

Anger over Trump’s tariff policy drove discontent in farm country, with Democrats ousting Republican Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and flipping the seat of Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson, who lost her bid to succeed retiring Sen. Joni Ernst.

Meanwhile, Latino voters, who were credited with helping propel Trump back into the White House in 2024, bolstered Democratic successes in Texas, scuttling GOP hopes of making good on the party’s mid-decade redistricting gambit.

Texas Republicans believed Latino voters would stick with the party this year when they redrew the state’s congressional map to create up to five pickup opportunities. But anger over the president’s immigration policies, coupled with economic anxiety, has driven Trump’s approval numbers among Latinos to historic lows.

In South Texas, a pair of Democratic incumbents — Reps. Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar — easily held on to their redrawn seats, while former Bexar County sheriff’s deputy Johnny Garcia prevailed over Air Force veteran Carlos De La Cruz in a district newly redrawn to elect a Republican. Democratic attorney and educator Katy Padilla Stout flipped the open 23rd District, which stretches across the state’s border with Mexico, and Tejano singer Bobby Pulido routed GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in another South Texas race.

The strength of the Democrats’ performance was evident in several under-the-radar races the party won in traditionally red districts, including Missouri’s 2nd District, where Republican Rep. Ann Wagner was ousted, and Indiana’s 5th, where Rep. Victoria Spartz lost reelection.

Speaker Mike Johnson, who crisscrossed the country to boost Republican candidates in the final weeks of the campaign, noted Tuesday night that history wasn’t on the GOP side: The president’s party almost always loses seats in a midterm election.

“From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history,” Johnson said in Shreveport, La. “It looks like history will be kept tonight.”

The new Democratic majority is expected to dedicate resources to investigating the activities of the Trump administration as well as the president.

The likely new Democratic chairman of the House Judiciary Committee is Maryland’s Jamie Raskin, while the Oversight and Government Reform panel is likely to be led by California Rep. Robert Garcia. Raskin and Garcia have already been busy making oversight requests of the administration.

For instance, the two lawmakers joined on a letter last week calling for the retention of conversations between the president and AI chatbots on matters of policy.

“The President and his advisors’ use of AI exposes the country to malign influence from unknown and unaccountable third parties. We already have ample evidence that AI chatbots can be manipulated to suit the commercial, political, or personal agendas of their designers​,” Raskin and Garcia wrote.

Beyond the oversight, Jeffries outlined last month some of his legislative priorities for the next Congress.

“I think we need to put money in the pockets of everyday Americans by doing things like expanding the Child Tax Credit, as well as the Earned Income Tax Credit​,” Jeffries told News12. “And, of course, we also need to end this war because the war has dramatically increased gas prices, fertilizer prices and diesel costs.​”

That was a reference to the military campaign against Iran, which appears likely to ratchet back up after the midterms.

I​n a pre-election interview with CNN, Jeffries said priorities that unite the Democratic Caucus include action on stopping the president’s sweeping application of tariffs, as well as on reversing cuts to Medicaid and extending Affordable Care Act tax credits.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6073. Can Washington Afford to Deter Chinese Cyber Activity?

Analysis: Can Washington Afford to Deter Chinese Cyber Activity?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

In August, the U.S. Justice Department and the FBI dismantled the online infrastructure behind two hacking platforms operated by a Chinese state-sponsored group. It had been targeting sensitive U.S. government networks since at least 2018. In October, the agencies seized hacking tools used by another such group whose operations the U.S. government had previously disrupted in 2024.

Washington can deny Beijing’s hackers access to harmful capabilities. But the longevity and resurgence of the hackers’ campaigns raise a hard truth: Disruption alone cannot reverse the strategic advantages generated by years of Chinese cyber activity.

In August, the U.S. Justice Department and the FBI dismantled the online infrastructure behind two hacking platforms operated by a Chinese state-sponsored group. It had been targeting sensitive U.S. government networks since at least 2018. In October, the agencies seized hacking tools used by another such group whose operations the U.S. government had previously disrupted in 2024.

Washington can deny Beijing’s hackers access to harmful capabilities. But the longevity and resurgence of the hackers’ campaigns raise a hard truth: Disruption alone cannot reverse the strategic advantages generated by years of Chinese cyber activity.

The conventional U.S. approach to cyber deterrence has treated Chinese operations as individual security incidents. But to deter China from accruing advantages through cyber activity, the United States must change the incentives of a vast hacking ecosystem built around the Chinese state in order to counteract its impacts on the United States’ military, technology, and trade.

A shift is now underway in Washington. In March, the U.S. government’s 2026 Cyber Strategy promised sustained and aggressive action through public-private partnerships, which would combine offensive and defensive capabilities with economic and legal countermeasures. Recent reports from the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) and Britain’s Royal United Services Institute similarly advocate for coordinating cyber operations with other instruments of state power.

Such proposals appear to recognize that disrupting individual operations has not changed China’s broader cyber behavior. But while combining instruments may help disrupt individual operations and parts of the ecosystem, they may still fail to credibly deter the broader pattern of activity that generates cumulative advantage.

Therein lies the more troubling possibility: that the United States cannot credibly deter the broad pattern of Chinese cyber activity at a price that it is prepared—or willing—to sustain.

China’s recent cyber campaigns have advantages beyond individual intrusions. In 2023, for example, the Volt Typhoon campaign secured access to U.S. infrastructure in Guam that would be critical for U.S. operations in a future Taiwan contingency. While the United States removed some of the original footholds, the Justice Department has warned that the target infrastructure is still vulnerable; in early 2025, security analysts found that a Volt Typhoon-linked group had steadily penetrated U.S. utilities through that year. Disrupting individual intrusions had not prevented China from prepositioning for future disruption.

The year after the Guam intrusion, a campaign attributed to the Salt Typhoon hacker network compromised U.S. telecommunications networks, allowing Chinese actors to collect sensitive information from surveillance systems. More than a year after the intrusion was first disclosed, the campaign was discovered to be surveilling congressional staffers’ communications. It is still unclear whether Salt Typhoon infrastructure has been removed from the affected networks or whether it continues to accumulate intelligence.

A broad campaign of deterrence has proved to be largely ineffective, but it was once possible to think in narrower terms. In 2015, then-U.S. President Barack Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that neither side would conduct or knowingly support cyber-enabled theft of intellectual property for commercial advantage. Security firms subsequently reported a decline in detected Chinese intrusions against U.S. companies (although the decline had begun before the agreement, and its causes remain contested).

The agreement did not end Chinese cyber espionage. It did, however, identify a relatively narrow category of conduct—commercial theft—that the two governments could explicitly agree to restrain, as opposed to the broader range of purposes that Chinese cyber operations now serve, from espionage to conflict prepositioning.

Washington no longer faces a discrete category of conduct around which to organize a deterrence effort. Today, it must determine which activities deserve a response, how much future risk they pose, and what consequences might discourage further operations. A response calibrated to an intrusion’s immediate effects may miss its future significance. Punishing every instance of access that might someday be used disruptively, meanwhile, would be difficult to sustain.

Similarly, punishing any single actor or intermediary that enables Chinese cyber operations is no longer enough to deter the wider ecosystem. Contractors disappear and reemerge frequently. The company disrupted in October provided hacking services to the People’s Liberation Army and the Ministry of State Security (MSS); others have conducted intrusions for both the MSS and the Ministry of Public Security. Rather than relying on single, self-contained operations, Chinese security organizations draw on overlapping external providers, creating an ecosystem that can regenerate operational capacity even amid disruptions.

Washington thinks offensive cyber power will restore deterrence. It’s mistaken.

Allies fear that Washington is retreating from leadership at the worst possible time.

For Washington, sanctions, export restrictions, criminal investigations, and public exposure could threaten the commercial interests and personal security of these actors. Rewards and protections encouraging people inside the enabling network to disclose information or defect, as proposed by the CFR report, could change incentives within the ecosystem, not merely punish its visible members. Pressure could make providers more cautious, expose links between companies and state agencies, and make operations harder to mount. At the state level, a credible threat of coordinated economic and diplomatic consequences might also discourage activities that Beijing considers too costly.

Yet such proposals contain significant shortcomings. Many enablers operate inside China, where they have little exposure to U.S. markets or financial systems, and their main sources of income come from state customers. In the past, sanctions have dismantled individual companies fronting the state. They would continue to have little lasting effect on companies that are dependent on Chinese security agencies, since Beijing can fund, protect, or replace providers when their work serves a strategic purpose.

Crucially, imposing costs on a contractor changes Beijing’s calculation only if the contractor’s financial, operational, or reputational losses degrade a longer-term strategic capability, threatens to expose other state-sponsored operations, or makes replacement offensive capabilities more costly for the wider ecosystem. If a state agency can absorb the loss and find another supplier, then Washington will have spent resources on punishing a node without changing the demand for its services. Previous attempts to identify and disrupt such valuable nodes have simply resulted in a temporary lull before resurgence.

To put meaningful pressure on Beijing, Washington would need to credibly signal that specific Chinese cyber activities would trigger costs substantial enough to change Chinese leaders’ calculations. That would require coordinated measures in more visible areas of strategic competition, such as restrictions on semiconductor exports or access to U.S. markets.

But China could retaliate in areas of competition where it retains leverage, such as by further restricting U.S. access to rare earth and critical mineral supplies, disrupting U.S. defense production. In that case, efforts to protect national security by deterring Chinese cyber activity could ultimately undermine it elsewhere.

Washington would thus need to accept immediate economic costs in return for uncertain deterrent effects for as long as necessary, when even sustained pressure may not stop the wider accumulation of access and intelligence. For the United States, China’s cyber operations may simply not hold enough strategic or political significance to warrant that economic price.

That leaves Washington with a dilemma. When espionage today can become disruption tomorrow, the value of deterring a wider range of cyber activity must be weighed against the costs of sustaining those restrictions and absorbing countermeasures. The challenge is to cast a wide enough net to address the sources of future risk while keeping threats specific and credible enough to influence behavior.

Accepting these risks does not have to mean abandoning deterrence; Washington can still seek to prevent China from using its access to U.S. infrastructure to disrupt essential services or pressure U.S. leaders during a crisis. But it should not confuse deterring a specific act with deterring the wider pattern of activity that accumulates strategic advantages over time.

Access may be the most valuable when it remains concealed, preserving China’s choice of whether and when to leverage it and leaving Washington to bear the costs of preparing for multiple possible outcomes. The more that Beijing believes Washington will tolerate continued accumulation, the greater its incentive to preserve that position and scale it—as the price for the United States only grows higher with time.

Ahana Datta Fasel is the author of Full Stack Spies: Cyber Espionage in the Age of US-China Competition (Hurst). She advises U.K. Research and Innovation on national security and defense.

#6070. Dem AG pulls off upset of sitting Republican governor after blistering campaign in key swing state

'Fox News @ Night' features a debate on California Governor Gavin Newsom declaring Democrats and the Democratic Socialists of America are aligned and breaks down a new survey on Americans' satisfaction with the economy.

Nevada Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has successfully ousted Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo in Nevada, a significant pickup for Democrats in the critical battleground state, The Associated Press projects.

Ford's defeat of Lombardo comes in one of the most closely watched gubernatorial races in the country.

Ford’s victory makes him Nevada’s first Black governor and gives Democrats control of the governor’s office for the first time since Lombardo defeated Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022.

Ford, who has served as Nevada’s attorney general since 2019, campaigned on affordability, housing, education, healthcare and protecting access to abortion. He argued that Nevada families were struggling with high housing costs, energy bills and other rising expenses under Lombardo and the Republican administration.

FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: THE TOP RACES TO WATCH AS 36 STATES CHOOSE THEIR NEXT GOVERNOR

Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, right, and Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford. (Carmen Mandato/Getty Images; Las Vegas Review-Journal file/Tribune News Service via Getty Images)

The result could also give Nevada Democrats unified control of state government depending on Tuesday night's election results, with the party already holding majorities in both chambers of the state Legislature. Ford will enter office with a legislative majority aligned with his agenda, although significant disagreements could remain over taxes, education spending, public safety and the state’s business climate.

Ford repeatedly criticized Lombardo for aligning himself with President Donald Trump and national Republicans. He argued that Nevada needed a governor who would challenge the administration on federal funding, immigration and voting rights while focusing on the state’s cost-of-living crisis.

The Republican incumbent defended his record on public safety, education, economic development and government spending. Lombardo argued that his administration had increased education funding, expanded workforce development and worked to diversify Nevada’s economy beyond tourism and gaming.

A BLUE WAVE IN GOVERNORS' MANSIONS COULD HURT FAMILIES MORE THAN A BLUE CONGRESS

Nevada Attorney General Aaron Ford smiles during his governorship campaign kickoff event at the East Las Vegas Community Center on Monday, July 28, 2025, in Las Vegas. (Madeline Carter/Las Vegas Review-Journal)

Lombardo also accused Ford of proposing costly new government programs without explaining how they would be financed. His campaign pointed to a campaign analysis estimating that fully implementing Ford’s platform could cost billions of dollars over four years.

Ford rejected that analysis, arguing that Lombardo’s administration had included spending mechanisms and assumptions that were not part of his actual proposals. Ford said his agenda could be accomplished through a combination of existing state resources, federal funding and policy changes.

Housing affordability was one of the defining issues of the campaign. Nevada has faced a shortage of affordable homes, particularly in the Las Vegas and Reno areas, while rising rents and mortgage rates have placed pressure on working- and middle-class residents.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo secured the Republican nomination for a second term. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

The candidates also clashed over energy costs, public education, crime, abortion, immigration and the state’s reliance on tourism and gaming.

Nevada’s growing energy demands, including those connected to data centers and other large industrial projects, became another major campaign issue. Lombardo promoted efforts to attract businesses and investment, while Ford argued that economic development should not result in higher costs for residents or additional pressure on the state’s infrastructure.

Ford will now face pressure to deliver on his campaign promises while governing a state with significant budget, housing, education and infrastructure challenges.

As attorney general, Ford frequently challenged Trump administration policies in court. His election is likely to make Nevada a more prominent Democratic counterweight to the federal government as the state moves toward the 2028 presidential election.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

#6069. Why Kushner and Witkoff Keep Failing

Argument: Why Kushner and Witkoff Keep Failing

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are unofficial presidential envoys, personally selected by U.S. President Donald Trump to handle critical negotiations over Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. While it’s safe to say neither was selected after a long and extensive search (Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff is a longtime friend and golfing buddy), let’s be charitable and assume that they have been genuinely trying to reach agreements that would advance U.S. interests. The question is: Why have they accomplished so little?

Look at the record: The supposed peace deal over Gaza is a sham, as Israel continues to bomb Gaza with impunity, expand its territorial control there, and limit relief aid while tolerating (if not actively helping) Israeli settlers’ violent campaign against Palestinians in the West Bank. Genuine peace may not have been their real objective, however, as Kushner and Witkoff are both ardent Israel supporters who were even less likely to put serious pressure on Israel than former U.S. President Joe Biden (which is saying something). In this view, the Gaza agreement was a Potemkin peace deal whose main goal was to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas and get the conflict off the front pages while tying Israel’s hands as little as possible. If so, then one might concede that they accomplished their objective. But if the goal was peace, they failed.

Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are unofficial presidential envoys, personally selected by U.S. President Donald Trump to handle critical negotiations over Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran. While it’s safe to say neither was selected after a long and extensive search (Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff is a longtime friend and golfing buddy), let’s be charitable and assume that they have been genuinely trying to reach agreements that would advance U.S. interests. The question is: Why have they accomplished so little?

Look at the record: The supposed peace deal over Gaza is a sham, as Israel continues to bomb Gaza with impunity, expand its territorial control there, and limit relief aid while tolerating (if not actively helping) Israeli settlers’ violent campaign against Palestinians in the West Bank. Genuine peace may not have been their real objective, however, as Kushner and Witkoff are both ardent Israel supporters who were even less likely to put serious pressure on Israel than former U.S. President Joe Biden (which is saying something). In this view, the Gaza agreement was a Potemkin peace deal whose main goal was to free Israeli hostages held by Hamas and get the conflict off the front pages while tying Israel’s hands as little as possible. If so, then one might concede that they accomplished their objective. But if the goal was peace, they failed.

Similarly, their efforts to negotiate an agreement with Iran before the war never went anywhere, in part because these two amateur diplomats apparently didn’t understand some critical technical details regarding Iran’s nuclear program but also because Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided to launch a war while talks were underway. As with Gaza, the negotiations may have been something of a sham from the start, intended not to reach a lasting agreement but to allow time to prepare for another round of war.

Russia’s war in Ukraine is still raging, too—a direct refutation of Trump’s campaign boast that he could end it in 24 hours. Witkoff and Kushner have met with Russian officials on multiple occasions and offered increasingly generous inducements, even as the administration keeps pressuring Kyiv to cut a deal. The result has been not peace but more war, including expanding attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine and Russia alike.

If judged by whether their efforts have led to peace, in short, Kushner and Witkoff are 0 for 3. To be fair, handling all three of these conflicts at once would tax the abilities of an Otto von Bismarck or a Henry Kissinger, and trying to conduct complex and difficult diplomacy on behalf of an erratic president who is more interested in appearances than achievements would be a challenge for any negotiator. But these handicaps don’t fully explain their repeated failures.

Trump’s son-in-law embodies the rise of a trend that threatens to ignite a new nuclear age.

One can think of several reasons why their efforts have been unsuccessful, but a big part of the problem is their overarching worldview. Kushner and Witkoff and Trump are all real estate developers who are preoccupied with making money. That’s the only thing that really matters to them, which is why Trump seems more interested in monetizing the presidency than he is in actually governing and why Kushner may have pocketed billions of dollars in secret payments from the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia (an accusation he denies). If you assume that everyone else is also on the make, then the way to get to yes is to offer your counterparts a sweet deal that will make them richer. In this world, everyone has their price, and the trick is to figure out what that price is and then convince them you can meet it.

This one-dimensional perspective was already evident in Trump’s first term. It lay behind Kushner’s belief that the key to Middle East peace was to ignore the Palestinian desire for statehood or political rights and focus instead on promoting business deals among Israel, some wealthy Gulf states, and (eventually) Saudi Arabia. That same instinct underlay Trump’s belief that he could get North Korean leader Kim Jong Un to give up his arsenal of nuclear weapons by offering an alluring vision of ritzy resorts and luxury condos along North Korean beaches, an idea later recycled as a potential blueprint for Gaza. And it is obviously central to recent attempts to persuade the Kremlin to end its war in Ukraine by buying some Russian diesel fuel, letting Russian companies help develop gas fields in Alaska, talking up lucrative future business deals, and ending Moscow’s economic isolation from the West.

The obvious flaw in this worldview is its failure to recognize that the top priority for smart political leaders isn’t money or wealth—it’s national security. Security is more important because without it, one’s wealth is vulnerable: Having all the money in the world is useless if someone stronger can take it from you. Look at what happened to Kuwait in 1990, when Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein decided to invade the wealthy emirate, simultaneously eliminating one of his main creditors and gaining control of resources that would have increased Iraq’s GDP by roughly 40 percent. And his gambit would have worked had a coalition of outside powers not ridden to Kuwait’s rescue.

Wealth is far from irrelevant, of course, and greed can be a powerful motivator, too. I don’t doubt that Russian President Vladimir Putin would be happy to pocket all those blandishments that Kushner and Witkoff keep dangling as part of an eventual peace deal in Ukraine. But if all he cared about were money, he wouldn’t have invaded Ukraine in the first place, and he wouldn’t have continued to wage war there at considerable economic and human cost. Unless and until the security concerns (whether exaggerated or not) that drove his decision to invade are met, offering him a bunch of economic goodies isn’t going to end the war.

The same is true for Kyiv, of course: If money were all that mattered, the smart move would be to accept the loss of Crimea and the Donbas and hold out for a big aid package to rebuild Ukraine’s shattered economy. But Ukrainians don’t want to surrender lands they regard as rightly theirs, even for a price. Equally important, they don’t want to live in fear of future Russian threats. Thus, a future peace arrangement would have to meet both sides’ security concerns as well as their economic desires.

Nations also care about preserving their identity and cultural autonomy, and those living under a foreign yoke often want to govern themselves. As a result, these groups will sometimes make enormous sacrifices to try to establish their own state. Palestinians won’t abandon their national identity or desire for political rights in exchange for a lucrative economic package (even assuming one were genuinely on offer), and neither will any number of other aspiring national movements. That same sense of national pride also helps explain why bombing other countries to topple a regime or get it to surrender rarely works, even when it is coupled with the prospect of future economic benefits. On the contrary, such actions tend to rally the population behind leaders who might otherwise lack broad support and make them even less willing to compromise.

International politics, in short, is not like real estate development because relations among states take place in an arena where there is no central authority and where some states have the ability and the will to use violence to get what they want. In such a world, states have powerful incentives to guarantee their own security first and then worry about how to become more prosperous. A solid grasp of how business works and experience negotiating complicated deals can be an asset in diplomacy (as former Secretaries of State George Shultz and James Baker demonstrated)—but only if you understand the critical differences between these two realms. Regrettably, Kushner and Witkoff (and Trump) show no sign of having understood the distinction or of having learned very much from their experiences to date. But they (or their families) are making some serious bank while these conflicts rage on, which may have been the real goal all along.

Stephen M. Walt is a columnist at Foreign Policy and the Robert and Renée Belfer professor of international relations at Harvard University. Walt is the author of The New Geopolitics, a five-part newsletter masterclass breaking down the biggest concepts you should use to navigate today’s world. #6066. The Quiet Revolution in U.S.-Cypriot Relations

Analysis: The Quiet Revolution in U.S.-Cypriot Relations

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Since the 1974 Turkish invasion of Cyprus, Washington has almost exclusively seen the island as a problem in need of solution. But that dynamic has now quietly changed. Over the past decade, the Republic of Cyprus (ROC) has positioned itself as a critical security partner for an increasingly receptive United States. The bilateral relationship has gradually expanded to include defense, trade, basing, military training and exercises, crisis-response cooperation, and regular strategic dialogue. Given Cyprus’s strategic location, it is perhaps surprising that the initial impetus for this growing security relationship came from Cyprus, not Washington.

In short, despite its ongoing division, Cyprus is emerging as a security producer for the United States and the West. For Nicosia, this relationship serves as an effective deterrent against any future Turkish threat, which remains the ROC’s primary security preoccupation. Beyond that, deepening ties with the United States help boost Cyprus’s international status and provide cover for its growing arms relationships and other security ties with other states, such as France and Israel. Turkey has watched these developments warily, though so far without a forceful response.

In short, despite its ongoing division, Cyprus is emerging as a security producer for the United States and the West. For Nicosia, this relationship serves as an effective deterrent against any future Turkish threat, which remains the ROC’s primary security preoccupation. Beyond that, deepening ties with the United States help boost Cyprus’s international status and provide cover for its growing arms relationships and other security ties with other states, such as France and Israel. Turkey has watched these developments warily, though so far without a forceful response.

Since 1974, the ROC has governed only the island’s southern two-thirds while enjoying near-universal recognition as the de jure government of the entire island (other than two sovereign British bases constituting less than 3 percent of the island). Turkey occupies the island’s northern third, which declared independence in 1983 as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC). Only Turkey recognizes the TRNC, and its military is believed to maintain 30,000-40,000 troops there. The overwhelmingly Greek Cypriot population of ROC-held territory numbers just under a million; the Turkish Cypriot population in the north is about a quarter that size.

During the Cold War, the ROC joined the Non-Aligned Movement as a founding member in 1961 and remained in the group until it joined the European Union in 2004, which forced it to abandon formal neutrality. Maintaining reasonably good ties with both Washington and Moscow made sense, as both permanent members of the U.N. Security Council would influence any settlement of the island’s division.

Even after securing EU membership, Cyprus’s ties to Moscow initially remained close. The United States, for its part, was wary of pursuing security ties with the ROC. Concerned that close relations with Cyprus would upset the Turks and jeopardize prospects for Cypriot reunification, Washington went so far as to put an arms embargo on the country in 1987.

Cyprus’s East-West balancing act began to change significantly in 2013, when the ROC elected the pro-Western Nicos Anastasiades as president, replacing his Moscow-friendly, anti-NATO predecessor, Demetris Christofias of the communist Progressive Party of Working People. Rather than wait for another attempt at reunification to transform Cyprus’s geopolitical position, Anastasiades sought to build a U.S.-Cypriot relationship. He pitched Washington on the island’s strategic location at the intersection of Europe and the Middle East, with ports, airfields, offshore energy resources, and diplomatic ties across the region.

Washington, perhaps increasingly skeptical that decades-old reunification efforts would ever bear fruit, responded in kind to Cypriot overtures. By 2014, then-Vice President Joe Biden had publicly described the bilateral relationship as a “strategic partnership.”

This mutual shift in outlook accelerated during the first Trump administration, likely reinforced by the collapse of the most recent diplomatic effort at reunification in July 2017. The result was a 2018 bilateral statement of intent that laid the groundwork for future security cooperation. The U.S. Congress followed with the 2019 Eastern Mediterranean Security and Energy Partnership Act, which formally declared Cyprus a “key strategic partner” and created a path toward suspending the 1987 U.S. arms embargo.

For the United States, the opening reflected a reconceptualization of the region, accelerated by a worsening relationship with Turkey in the 2010s.

Former Assistant Secretary of State for Eurasian Affairs A. Wess Mitchell, widely viewed as the chief architect of the shift, argued in 2018 congressional testimony that Washington’s thinking about the region had grown stale. The United States, he said, had for decades mistakenly treated the Eastern Mediterranean as settled terrain anchored by Turkey while reducing Cyprus merely to a matter of reunification talks. In Mitchell’s vision, the Eastern Mediterranean was an “emerging maritime frontier” warranting greater attention. Greece and Cyprus, he reasoned, offered the United States strategic opportunities while also providing a hedge against an increasingly erratic Turkey.

For Cyprus, however, the reason for turning toward Washington wasn’t merely strategic; it was existential. Nicosia was seeking a suspension of Washington’s arms embargo, but more than that, it wanted a sense of strategic belonging. As the lone EU member outside both NATO and NATO’s Partnership for Peace program, which allows non-NATO governments to build a bilateral relationship with the alliance, Cyprus has tried to shed its status as Europe’s “half-in” member.

The ROC’s president, Nikos Christodoulides, has gone beyond his predecessors in that regard, saying repeatedly that he wants Cyprus inside NATO. Christodoulides knows that, given Turkey’s veto, that is a nearly inconceivable prospect absent a Cyprus settlement agreement. Nevertheless, he has cast cooperation with Washington as a means of bringing the Cypriot National Guard, as the Cypriot army is called, up to alliance standards.

Cooperation with the United States has helped professionalize the Cypriot military and upgrade Cyprus’s military infrastructure. Cypriot and American troops now train together, including by conducting special operations exercises beyond emergency rescue drills. U.S. Navy SEALs and the Cypriot navy’s underwater team conducted joint maritime counterterrorism and ship-boarding training in 2021 and 2024. Since 2022, Cyprus has partnered with the New Jersey National Guard for joint training and disaster response. In December 2024, Congress made Cyprus eligible for U.S.-financed multilateral training—the only non-NATO, non-Partnership for Peace country with this status.

Through the U.S. European Command (EUCOM), Washington funded a roughly $588,000 assessment in 2025 to bring Andreas Papandreou Air Base up to NATO standards, recommending a new heavy-lift apron and expanded runway, which Cyprus will finance. A new EUCOM-funded heliport at Evangelos Florakis Naval Base will accommodate large Chinook-type helicopters, and the Ministry of Defense is studying expansion to host eight large warships. Limassol has become a routine U.S. Navy port of call, hosting 22 vessels since 2022, including 15 since 2024.

Cyprus has expanded its cooperation with the United States by taking on regional responsibilities that leverage its strategic location while seeking to avoid provoking Turkey. The country’s national plan enables rapid noncombatant evacuation, opening ports and airports for civilians fleeing conflicts. In 2024, U.S. Marines and Ospreys deployed to Papandreou Air Base for possible evacuations from Lebanon, and Cyprus served as a transit point for those leaving Israel during the June 2025 Iran conflict.

Beyond evacuations, Cyprus has supported humanitarian deliveries to Gaza in partnership with the U.N., sending more than 37,000 metric tons of supplies. Its location at the crossroads of Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East has also made it a regional training hub. By 2025, the U.S.-funded Cyprus Center for Land, Open Seas, and Port Security  in Larnaca had trained more than 2,000 officials from more than 20 countries in security and counterterrorism.

Of course, the question of Turkey is never far from Cypriot calculations. Closer ties to Washington plainly serve Nicosia’s concerns about its neighbor.

An example of how U.S. ties provide indirect deterrence is found in Cyprus’s recently acquired air-defense capability. When Cyprus sought to field Russian S-300 air-defense missiles in 1997, Ankara threatened to bomb the batteries before they were fully deployed. Washington defused that crisis by pressing Nicosia to transfer the S-300s to Greece, which then stored them unobtrusively on Crete.

When Cyprus purchased the Israeli Barak MX system in 2024, however, Turkey warned of dangerous consequences but never threatened direct military intervention to block Cyprus from deploying it. Several factors may explain Turkey’s more restrained response in 2024, but Cyprus’s new security relationship with the United States, including the limited but consistent presence of U.S. troops in the ROC, is certainly among the most important.

Meanwhile, Israel also has emerged as a key security partner for Cyprus. Although Cyprus’s security relationship with Israel predates the acceleration of its security ties with Washington, the latter has accelerated expansion of the former.

Beyond bilateral Israeli-Cypriot relations, Cyprus, Israel, and Greece hold regular joint summits and cooperate in several areas, including energy. That triangular relationship has made the Turks uneasy, but the United States has blessed it and, since Trump’s first term, occasionally participates in it, creating a grouping known as the “3+1.” Cyprus has also built important ties with other regional actors, including Egypt, Jordan, and several Persian Gulf states.

This emerging strategy carries risks for both Washington and Nicosia. The island now hosts more arms than at any point in decades, and each proposed U.S. transfer forces a judgment about whether additional weaponry and military infrastructure projects bolster stability or erode it. Perhaps tellingly, Washington has yet to act on a Cypriot request for excess defense articles made more than a year ago.

The broader challenge for the United States is to draw on Cyprus’s location and strengthen its military without stoking Turkish fears to the point of reigniting long-dormant hostilities, an outcome that is squarely against U.S. interests. For Cyprus, the corresponding danger is losing control over a relationship with a far more powerful partner, as a U.S. military increasingly comfortable operating from the island may eventually seek to stage operations from it, drawing the ROC into conflicts that it would prefer to avoid. Conversely, Cyprus has to reckon with the possibility that a more isolationist United States might abandon the security relationship altogether.

Cyprus’s deepening ties with Israel sharpen that exposure. As relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated since Oct. 7, 2023, Cyprus risks becoming another arena of Turkish-Israeli friction, alongside Syria and the Horn of Africa.

Closer alignment with Washington and Israel also draws the island nearer to the confrontation with Iran: In March 2026, a drone most likely launched by Hezbollah from Lebanon struck a sovereign British base in the island’s south, just a few miles from ROC territory—a reminder that Cyprus can be targeted in conflicts not of its own making. Nicosia must therefore work to keep Israeli-Turkish tensions, and the wider Iranian threat, from boiling over onto the island.

Nicosia wants Washington to see it as a natural ally, even absent a treaty to that effect, as well as a security producer rather than a divided country whose enduring security problem overwhelms all other considerations. To that end, it has positioned itself as a friendly, democratic government in a tough region that can help evacuate Americans from Middle Eastern wars, train regional security officials, host naval vessels, support humanitarian missions, counter illicit finance, obstruct terrorism, and operate alongside Western militaries.

Still, that transformation remains incomplete. Cyprus may be an unsinkable aircraft carrier, but the United States is still deferential to Turkish sensibilities regarding Cyprus, even if it is much less deferential than it was a decade ago, and for now has not sought to exploit Cyprus’s full military potential. Cyprus, too, likes to emphasize that it does not allow foreign militaries to stage offensive operations from its territory, a position most recently reiterated at the outset of the Iran war.

Cyprus is not a formal U.S. ally, hosts no permanent U.S. bases, and remains outside NATO. The island’s unresolved division will likely continue to constrain how far military cooperation with the United States can go. Should the prospect of reunification vanish altogether, the strategic ambiguity that has allowed the partnership to deepen quietly may grow harder to sustain, pressing Washington to weigh Cypriot opportunity against Turkish sensitivities more openly than it has so far.

But Nicosia no longer appears willing to let that dispute define the boundaries and ambition of its foreign policy. After decades of waiting for geopolitics to change its circumstances, Cyprus is now actively using its geography and growing strategic importance to change its geopolitics.

Alan Makovsky is a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, a Washington-based think tank. He was formerly an official at the State Department and a senior staff member at the House Foreign Affairs Committee.

Jonah Brody is a policy analyst at the Jewish Institute for National Security of America.

#6064. How Russia Sees the World Now

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

DMITRY ADAMSKY is Professor at Reichman University and an Associate with the Project on Managing the Atom at Harvard University. He is the author of The Russian Way of Deterrence: Strategic Culture, Coercion, and War.

The Kremlin’s New Mental Map Is Changing the War in Ukraine—and the Confrontation With the West

In 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine, the Kremlin’s strategic thinking was shaped around several core ideas. It viewed the United States as its principal geopolitical rival, an adversary that had encouraged Kyiv to impose strategic defeat on Moscow. It considered Europe and NATO largely as an extension of American power. And it saw nuclear muscle flexing as efficient means to exert coercive pressure.

Today, after nearly five years of war, and 22 months of the second Trump administration, the mental map guiding Russian strategy has changed. First, Russia now sees Europe, instead of the United States, as its principal geopolitical adversary, a shift that has driven Russia’s defense establishment to call for an approach known as “castling” to deal with the main threats. Related to this, Moscow now attributes new strategic agency to Europe itself because of the dramatic military modernization taking place in many European countries and the growing interest among some European leaders in developing or extending their own nuclear deterrent. A third shift concerns Russia’s theory of deterrence: Moscow’s traditional understanding of nuclear coercion is giving way to new thinking about nonnuclear strategic deterrence using advanced conventional weapons systems aimed at Europe.

These new lines of thought, which have gained prominence among influential defense intellectuals and policy experts close to the Kremlin over the past year do not need to be endorsed in formal security doctrine to matter. As the past decade has shown, ideas circulating within Russia’s national security establishment have shaped how officials frame problems, define options, and ultimately make major strategic choices. The three recent shifts in Russian strategic thinking will likely play an important part in how Moscow approaches any negotiation to end the war, as well as how it manages future escalation and competition with Europe and the United States.

As the Trump administration steps up its efforts to engage Moscow, it is now negotiating with a Russian leadership whose strategic mindset has evolved considerably since 2022. For the United States, understanding Russia’s new mental map will not only be crucial to any attempt to find an off-ramp with Moscow. It will also be essential to reducing the risk of inadvertent escalation between Russia and Europe and to ensuring strategic stability on the continent in the years to come.

One of the most notable trends in Russian strategic thought over the past year has been the emergence of the idea of “castling.” A term borrowed from chess, castling in geopolitics describes the repositioning of forces and resources to optimize a state’s strategic posture. Moscow’s defense experts have used the concept to describe a strategy for dealing with a new reality: for the first time since World War II, they have argued, Europe, rather than the United States, has become Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary. According to this view, European countries are now the principal source of Ukraine’s military capacity, political resolve, and strategic resilience; it is Europe and not the United States that has made Ukraine its proxy and is encouraging Kyiv to pursue Moscow’s strategic defeat.

As a consequence, Moscow must direct coercive pressure at Europe—its elites, its decision-making centers, and its critical infrastructure. By doing so, Russia can instill into Europe’s calculus what theorists in Moscow call a “deterring fear”: a European reluctance to antagonize Russia through further support to Ukraine. Such action, they argue, can also rebuild Russian credible deterrence for long-term competition with the West, which is now centered on Europe.

Castling does not imply a change in Russia’s overall objectives, which remain the same as those invoked by Russian President Vladimir Putin at the time of the 2022 invasion. These include banning NATO enlargement to Ukraine and other former Soviet republics; rolling back NATO’s eastern flank; and restricting NATO military exercises, as well as the conventional and nuclear deployments of NATO members, near Russian borders. The difference is that Russian coercion must now be aimed at Europe rather than the United States to achieve these objectives.

Along with this revised assessment of Europe, Russian strategists have interpreted the Trump administration’s own strategic stance as evidence that Asia has replaced Europe as the principal theater of U.S. strategic competition. They point to the administration’s reluctance to back Ukraine, its desire to terminate the war, and its continued overtures to the Kremlin. The administration’s decision in mid-October to provide sanctions relief to Russia and apply new pressure on Ukraine amplify this view in Moscow. Russian strategists also assume Washington seeks to solidify its control of the Western Hemisphere and views China, not Russia, as its primary long-term adversary.

Moscow believes that Washington is thus seeking to reduce its commitments in secondary theaters—particularly Europe and the Middle East—in order to concentrate political, military, and organizational resources on Beijing. As Russia sees it, the new American assertiveness in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Caribbean is unsurprising. By contrast, the current war in Iran—the biggest U.S. military engagement in recent years—has been read in Moscow as an unintended deviation from the new direction of U.S. policy, one that Washington seeks to correct as soon as possible. Whether this reading reflects actual American intentions matters less than that it has become a prevailing understanding in Moscow.

A related trend in Russian discourse is a growing fixation on what defense experts refer to as Europe’s “nuclear curiosity” and new military assertiveness near Russian borders. Specifically, Russian strategists have been concerned by the French and British governments’ modernization of their nuclear programs and apparent readiness to wield them more assertively. Moscow has also noted the prospect of French or British nuclear guarantees extending to European states and nonnuclear European capitals considering the development of nuclear options of their own.

Russian sources identify Germany, Poland, and the Nordic-Baltic states as “nuclear curious,” whether in pursuing nuclear-threshold status or seeking protection under French and British nuclear umbrellas. In this regard, comments by Polish officials in early 2026 expressing support for a Polish nuclear deterrent have been particularly noted. Russian strategists have also closely monitored discussions by Paris and London about offering extended deterrence to the continent as an alternative to the U.S. umbrella.

From Moscow’s perspective, any new attempt by a European state to become a nuclear power would cross a redline and could potentially create a casus belli. Moreover, Europe’s growing assertiveness on nuclear issues is happening in parallel with the deployment of conventional deep-strike precision weapons near Russian borders. For NATO, this more active European posture mitigates the risk of Washington shifting away from its European allies, but to Moscow it signals that Europe could potentially undertake strikes aimed at disarming Russia’s nuclear arsenal or decapitating its leadership.

To Russian analysts, these various developments also suggest Europe’s growing strategic autonomy from the United States. Traditionally, Moscow has viewed Europe largely as a “parking lot” for U.S. forces: a region of the world that is relevant but strategically subordinate to Washington. That assumption is changing. Along with the perception that Europe is now Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary, the continent’s increasing strategic autonomy, including on both nuclear and conventional issues, has become a crucial variable in Russia’s calculus. According to Moscow’s defense intellectuals, Russia may need to change its posture to contain this trend, including by seeking new tools to keep Europe at bay and to coerce it below the nuclear threshold.

To align with Russia’s new mental map, Russian defense intellectuals and military officers have been examining how to make Moscow’s coercive threats more effective. During the first years of the war, Russia’s nuclear muscle flexing and hybrid warfare failed to prevent Ukraine’s allies from funneling financial support, military aid, and targeting intelligence to Kyiv. This approach also failed to deter Ukraine’s land incursions into Russia and strikes on symbolic Russian targets and Russian strategic infrastructure, let alone compel Kyiv to surrender.

Today, NATO is preoccupied with Russia’s escalating cross-domain coercion, or what U.S. and European analysts call hybrid warfare. But that is only one part of the Russian approach. As Moscow concentrates on Europe as the new primary threat, it is also drawing on new tools of coercion that Russian experts call nonnuclear strategic deterrence. For Russian military authors, NNSD involves using advanced conventional capabilities, including precision-guided weapons, drones, ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missile systems, as well as “weapons based on new physical principles”—a Russian catchall term for electromagnetic-pulse and high-power microwave weapons to deter and compel adversaries.

Conceptually, NNSD belongs to what Russian experts refer to as the “art of strategic gestures,” a euphemism for using, or threatening to use, nuclear and nonnuclear capabilities to deter and coerce an adversary. The concept is not new. Since the early years of this century, Russian strategists have tried to develop conventional alternatives to nuclear deterrence. But until the full-scale war in Ukraine began, in 2022, these ideas remained underdeveloped. NNSD has emerged from the lessons learned during the conflict.

From the outset of the war, Russia used tactical ballistics, cruise missiles, and hypersonic capabilities, which it has paired with drones and maneuver warfare. But even when coupled with the threat of nuclear coercion, this approach underdelivered, in the view of many Russian analysts. As a result, as the war has become entrenched, in particular since 2024, Moscow has shifted its focus to more advanced ballistic salvo waves, including strikes using Russia’s intermediate-range Oreshnik ballistic missile.

Drawing on this experience, Russian military theoreticians center NNSD on using massive, deep, precision strikes against the adversary’s critical military, political, and economic infrastructure. The strategy, they suggest, should be aimed not only at Ukraine but also at its European supporters. Although the exact contours of NNSD are still emerging, the concept appears to be more escalatory than the hybrid warfare and deniable asymmetric campaigns that Russia is currently pursuing in Europe.

This is more than a peripheral theoretical discussion. There are already indications that NNSD has gained traction among Russia’s senior military officers: for example, since 2025, the flagship journal of Russia’s general staff, Military Thought, has published several articles on the subject. All the branches of the Russian military are also developing their own versions of NNSD and are seeking to claim a comparative advantage in its execution. This interservice competition may increasingly normalize what constitutes acceptable coercion below the nuclear threshold and shape targeting priorities, as well as escalation management.

As the Kremlin sees it, the war in Ukraine began as an attempt to impel Europe to reshape its security architecture. Yet the strategic landscape confronting Moscow today may look even more threatening than the one it sought to change in 2022. Washington needs to recognize that the Kremlin regards Ukraine not as a discrete conflict but as part of a broader struggle over Europe’s strategic order. Any U.S.-led effort to broker an off-ramp in Ukraine will need to reckon with Moscow’s emerging castling logic and its mounting anxieties about Europe. A settlement that addresses the immediate battlefield while leaving Moscow’s wider frictions with Europe untouched is likely to provide only a temporary pause in this larger conflict. Washington needs to understand that Russia’s nonnuclear coercion has become a part of its ongoing deterrence strategy against Europe rather than simply a feature of the war itself.

Even if Moscow engages in negotiations to end the war, it is likely to continue using military coercion against Ukraine, as well as Europe. It will do so for several reasons: to align the terms of the settlement with Russian interests, to refine Russia’s emerging theory of nonnuclear strategic deterrence, and to force Europe to adopt a different security architecture. Russia may therefore undertake precision strikes on critical infrastructure, and even possible decapitation attempts, as well as calibrated attacks of varying intensity in Ukraine, alongside diplomatic engagement. By using such tactics, Moscow will be seeking not only to gain leverage in negotiations with Kyiv but also to restore its strategic deterrence with Europe. In response, Europe, doubting the credibility of the Trump administration’s commitments and seeking to demonstrate its own resolve, may decide to escalate.

Washington should thus be prepared for the possibility that stepped-up efforts to terminate the war may coincide with heightened security risks in Europe. Given that the dynamic between Europe and Russia is now characterized by pervasive mutual suspicion, conspiracy theories, and expectations of war, there is a growing danger of inadvertent escalation. Actions by either side that are intended as limited coercion, signaling, or leverage might be misread, thus triggering a self-reinforcing action-reaction cycle in which each side’s effort to restore deterrence instead erodes it. Paradoxically, this dynamic could emerge precisely at the moment when all sides—including the Kremlin—are seeking an off-ramp. Both Europe and Russia risk crossing a “culmination point of coercion,” beyond which any additional threats to use force, or its actual use, could expand the war further.

For Russia and Europe, then, the main challenge will be to bolster deterrence without crossing this tipping point. For Washington, the primary task is not only to mediate the substance of a deal but also to learn how to choreograph negotiations amid ongoing military action. It will be imperative for U.S. officials to anticipate coercive moves by all sides without mistaking them for a rejection of diplomacy—and without allowing them to derail negotiations. Washington will need to help both Europe and Russia contain their use of coercion before the security dilemma locks them into a dangerous escalatory spasm.

#6063. Soviet Nostalgia Is a Geopolitical Dead End

Argument: Soviet Nostalgia Is a Geopolitical Dead End
